title: Terminology and notation
text: The notation below is used throughout the collection. Numerical interpretation depends on the target orientation, posterior law and eligible report family. Each application specifies these assumptions for its own examples.

title: Terminology and notation
text:
Targets and posterior uncertainty


Unit; criterion k

A firm, school, site or other entity included in the comparison population. A criterion is a target on which the report is evaluated. Units outside this population remain unassessed.
Examples: Multiple criteria · Supplied summaries

θᵢ

The oriented target for unit i. Larger values denote higher reporting priority. This orientation is specified substantively and need not correspond to better outcomes or greater need.
Examples: Two-unit comparison · Alabama counties

Posterior

The distribution of target values conditional on the stated data and model. Reported posterior risk is an expectation under this distribution. Its calculation does not establish calibration in an external population.
Examples: Posterior shrinkage · Posterior inputs

πᵢⱼ

The posterior probability of a specified direction, such as Pr(θᵢ > θⱼ). It concerns the joint distribution of two targets; a marginal interval for one unit does not determine it.
Examples: Direction probabilities · Interval overlap

eᵢⱼ⁽ᵏ⁾

The probability that stating i above j is wrong on criterion k. Under the zero-margin weak-error convention, exact equality counts as a wrong strict direction. The forward and reverse errors can therefore sum to more than one when equality has positive probability. Event conventions and comparison margins are specified with the input.
Examples: Pairwise decisions · Posterior equality

Marginal interval

A posterior interval for an individual target at a specified probability level. Its level is marginal rather than simultaneous across units. Overlap of two such intervals is distinct from their direction probability.
Example: Report-card summaries

Expected rank

The posterior average position of a unit under a specified rank and tie convention. Ordering these averages gives one possible ranking and can define a fixed-order report family.
Example: Alternative ranking summaries

title: Terminology and notation
text:
Grade reports, disclosure and error


Grade report g

An ordered partition of the included units, with grade 1 at the high-priority end. Different grades state a direction; a shared grade withholds a comparison without asserting equality. Allocation requires an additional decision rule.
Examples: Report construction · Allocation objectives

n, M

The number of included units and their M = n(n − 1)/2 unordered pairs. Each cross-grade pair contributes one stated direction.
Example: Report-family counts

N, s = N/M

The number of stated pairs and the disclosure share. The remaining M − N pairs are withheld.
Example: Disclosure from tier sizes

Eₖ

The posterior expected number of wrong stated directions on criterion k, obtained by summing directional error probabilities over the stated pairs. Joint correctness is a separate probability.
Example: Expected and realised errors

Eₖ/N

The expected wrong share among stated pairs of a fixed report. It is NA: no disclosure when N = 0.
Example: Error-rate denominators

DRₖ = Eₖ/M

The expected wrong count per possible pair. Withholding can reduce this rate by reducing the set of stated directions. The criterion subscript is usually omitted in single-criterion examples.
Example: Error-rate denominators

τ

The cost per withheld pair when a wrong stated direction costs one. Weighted risk is R_τ = (E_w + τ(M − N))/M.
Example: Reporting risk

λ, ϕ

KRW’s reward for a correct direction and the informed share in their stipulated audience model. The conversion is τ = λ/(1 + λ) and ϕ = 1 − 2τ. The positive-cost audience range is 0 < λ ≤ 1, 0 < τ ≤ 1/2 and 0 ≤ ϕ < 1. Equivalence of optimal reports requires the stated common-posterior, tie-free and common-family conditions.
Examples: Loss-scale conversion · Equivalent reporting losses



The inequality E_w ≤ τN holds for a loss-minimising report when its eligible family includes the all-withheld report. It does not apply automatically to an arbitrary fixed report or rule. Shared grades, exact equality of latent values and equal-risk optimisation solutions refer to distinct properties.

title: Terminology and notation
text:
Report families and comparisons


Family; grade cap

The set of reports eligible for optimisation. Examples include all reports with at most a specified number of grades and contiguous cuts of a fixed order. An optimum within one order has this restricted scope. Equal order scores may be required to remain together.
Examples: Report families · Computation methods

Frontier

The lower convex boundary of expected wrong counts against disclosure in the specified family, allowing randomisation over complete reports. A point on an edge may be unattainable by a single report. Reports optimal at the same τ can have different disclosures.
Examples: Error–disclosure frontier · Comparison constraints

ψ

The probability of selecting the higher-disclosure complete report in a mixture of two frontier reports. The resulting expected disclosure describes a randomised reporting rule; it need not correspond to a deterministic intermediate grade vector.
Example: Mixtures of reports

wₖ, E_w = ∑ₖ wₖEₖ

Nonnegative criterion error weights summing to one, and the weighted expected wrong count. These weights apply to directional losses. Coefficients of a scalar composite target have a separate role.
Examples: Common grades · Composite targets

qₖ

An expected-error budget, expressed in count form as Eₖ ≤ qₖN. With no stated directions both sides are zero, although the error share is undefined. Some applications use budgets only to evaluate the displayed report; others use them to restrict selection.
Examples: Budget-constrained families · Case-report checks

Δₖ

The risk of a common report on criterion k minus that criterion’s minimum risk under the same loss and feasible family. Optimisation bounds give an interval when the criterion-specific minimum is not established. Differences between settings or nonnested families need not have this interpretation.
Example: Criterion-specific excess risk

Selection belief; evaluation law

The distribution used to select a report and the distribution used to evaluate that fixed report. Evaluation under a different law gives a different expected loss, even when the grade vector is unchanged.
Examples: Alternative evaluation laws · Selection-draw evaluation

Joint correctness

The probability that all stated directions are correct together. Pairwise probabilities and expected wrong counts alone do not determine this event probability. Composite targets similarly require the relevant joint-law information.
Example: Limits of pairwise probabilities

Simulation error

Numerical uncertainty due to a finite set of posterior draws. Independent draws and dependent chains require different variance calculations and diagnostics. Increasing the number of draws reduces numerical error under the supplied law without establishing the adequacy of the model.
Examples: Independent-draw error · Dependent-draw error



Across repeated datasets, the mean of realised error fractions, the ratio of expected wrong and stated counts, and the mean posterior-reported share define different summaries. Their denominators and conditioning must therefore be specified. Averaging across reports illustrates these distinctions, and the case-report tool records the quantities used in its reporting account. None of these summaries alone establishes external calibration.

title: Alternative rankings from a posterior distribution
text: A posterior distribution supports several ranking summaries. The slope chart compares orderings by posterior mean, expected rank and probability of membership in a specified top group. Expected rank is the posterior average position, with rank 1 assigned to the largest value. Differences in posterior dispersion or shape can produce different pairwise orders under these summaries. Rank distributions describe the remaining uncertainty in each unit’s position. A finite three-unit distribution and a simulated league illustrate these distinctions, including the effect of changing the measurement scale on rankings by posterior mean.

title: Alternative rankings from a posterior distribution
text:
Numerical illustrations

Three-unit law, posterior mean. A has the largest posterior mean, a value it takes in neither state, yet its expected rank, 2.4, is the worst: A is first with probability .3 and last otherwise. The two orders differ on 2 of the 3 pairs.
Three-unit law, first place. B is the most likely to be first (.7); C never is.
Three-unit law, √θ. On the square-root scale A’s posterior mean falls to 1.34, below B’s 2.00 and C’s 1.73, so the first column now follows the expected ranks: 0 of the 3 pairs differ.
League, expected rank. U13, a small unit with posterior SD .120, is 6th by posterior mean but 8th by expected rank (9.59): the large units U06 and U24 pass it. Its 90% rank interval runs from rank 1 to rank 24. The two orders differ on 6 of the 435 pairs.
League, top ten. U21 is the unit most often in the top ten in 4,000 Monte Carlo draws (.96; one standard error is below .01), ahead of U26 (.94), which has the largest posterior mean. Two units are never in the top ten.
League, exp(10θ). On this scale U13 climbs from 6th to 3rd by posterior mean (4.09), and that order puts 40 of the 435 pairs differently from the expected rank.







The three-unit law is specified directly and the league’s posterior is set by hand for teaching; postrank fits neither. Rankings by posterior means appear in Kline, Rose and Walters (2024), Section IV.B and the notes to Figure 2C, where empirical Bayes posterior means are coarsened into deciles and quartiles; talk slide 59 sets such rules beside their grades for the firms. Their Section II.F names the expected rank.

title: Normal–normal posterior shrinkage
text: Under a normal likelihood and a common normal prior, each posterior mean is a precision-weighted average of the estimate and the prior mean. The two precisions are the inverse squared standard error and the inverse prior variance. The posterior mean minimises posterior expected squared error. Each row displays an estimate θ̂ᵢ in vermillion and its posterior mean in navy. Less precise estimates receive greater shrinkage towards the prior mean. Unequal sampling precisions can therefore change the order of the units; equal precisions preserve the order under this model.

title: Normal–normal posterior shrinkage
text:
Numerical illustrations

Prior SD .15. Small units move .64 of the way to 0, medium units .31 and large units .10, so greater shrinkage towards 0 changes the order of imprecise units relative to precise units: in this draw the order changes for 37 of the 435 pairs.
Prior SD .05. A narrower prior increases shrinkage: small units move .94, large units .50, and in this draw 71 of the 435 pairs change order.
Every SE .10. A common SE gives a common retained share, .69, for every unit: no lines cross, and 0 of the 435 pairs change order.
Against the true values. In this draw the average squared distance to the true values (crosses) falls from .0163 to .0096 and the spread from .162 to .098, below the truth’s .149; yet 14 of 30 units end farther (ringed).
Too narrow a prior. A prior too narrow for these true values can even raise the average: at prior SD .02, .0197 against the estimates’ .0163 in this draw, and .0191 against .0175 over many draws.







Kline, Rose and Walters (2024), KRW, estimate their prior from all the firms (section III, slide 49); it is not normal, depends on each firm’s SE (section V.B) and, for race, puts all its weight on positive gaps. So State Farm’s race estimate of −.544 (SE .444) has a posterior mean of .155 (90% interval .014 to .342, from a smoothed version of KRW’s posteriors). In their data, ranks from linear (James–Stein-type) shrinkage “perform substantially worse than naively ranking the point estimates” (section V.E). The postrank theory book (ch. 20, “Empirical Bayes specification”) sets out their prior; the normal prior here is a teaching simplification. The data describe KRW’s correspondence experiment, not any firm’s current conduct.

title: Expected errors in a strict ranking
text: A strict ranking states a direction for every unordered pair of units. For n units it therefore makes M = n(n − 1)/2 statements, represented by the cells of a triangle. A statement that i exceeds j is wrong with posterior probability 1 − πᵢⱼ, where πᵢⱼ is the probability that i has the larger true value. Summing these error probabilities gives the posterior expected number of incorrect statements. In the examples, uncertain comparisons are concentrated among nearby ranks, although two imprecise units can remain difficult to order even when widely separated in the displayed ranking (The matrix of pairwise posterior probabilities).

title: Expected errors in a strict ranking
text:
Numerical illustrations

97 firms. Kline, Rose and Walters’ (KRW) firms, ranked by posterior mean, make 4,656 claims; the posterior expected wrong count is 1,249, more than one in four. Ranked by estimate they expect 1,395 (the two orders disagree on 639 pairs); KRW find the posterior-mean order close to their best strict ranking (Section V.E), but that is not a general rule. Here 35 claims sit above one half.
Top 10 by posterior mean. 45 claims, 18.22 expected wrong. The scale table sets them beside the 17,014,861 claims of a ranking of the case study’s 5,834 California schools (elementary-type schools with at least 30 students counted).
Six sites. 15 claims, .7194 expected wrong. The highest dot, C above D, is a claim between neighbours, wrong with probability .362.
League of 30. 435 claims; 94.48 expected wrong, 102.2 by estimate (37 pairs differ). Only a simulation knows the true values: 88 claims are wrong against them in this draw, 80.69 on average.







KRW’s race card at λ = 1 is also a full ranking, in a slightly different order, so it expects 1,248 wrong claims where the posterior-mean order expects 1,249 (KRW’s archived reward path). The expected count is a sum of probabilities over all the claims, not a list of particular claims. The data describe KRW’s correspondence experiment, not any firm’s current conduct. Data: Kline, Rose and Walters (2024), doi:10.1257/aer.20230700; deposit doi:10.3886/E198284V1; CC-BY-NC as stated by the deposit (no version), noncommercial use only. title: The matrix of pairwise posterior probabilities
text: The cell in row i and column j contains πᵢⱼ = Pr(θᵢ > θⱼ ∣ Y). Since equality has posterior probability zero in this example, the transposed cell contains 1 − πᵢⱼ. Under independent normal posteriors, ordering units by their posterior means places many of the less certain comparisons near the diagonal. The width of this region also reflects differences in posterior precision. Alternative orderings permute each unit’s row and column together, leaving the underlying probabilities unchanged. The matrix thus distinguishes posterior uncertainty from the choice of an ordering for presentation.

title: The matrix of pairwise posterior probabilities
text:
Numerical illustrations

Six sites, by posterior mean. C above D, .638, is the least certain direction, and its cell is next to the diagonal; A above B (.812) and E above F (.856) follow. Below the diagonal each cell is one minus its mirror: D above C is .362.
Six sites, by label. The same matrix, with C above D still at .638: the labels already follow the posterior means.
League, by label. Of 435 pairs, the least certain, U19 above U25 at .502, sits 6 cells from the diagonal. None of these 10 least certain pairs is next to the diagonal; the farthest is 26 cells away.
League, by posterior mean. The middle-blue cells now form a band: U19 above U25 is next to the diagonal, and so are 8 of these 10 least certain pairs; the farthest is 2 cells away.
Two imprecise units. At prior SD .10 the cell in row U22, column U25 is 5 cells from the diagonal, yet its probability is only .528: both are small units with posterior SD .089.







The six sites are fictional after-school sites, A to F, from postrank’s tutorial data: their normal posteriors for the reading score are set by hand and taken as given. An evaluation office grades them to set the order of its visits. The league is that of Ranking noisy estimates, with the posterior of normal–normal posterior shrinkage. Two imprecise units can have direction probabilities near one half even when they are far apart in the ranking. Kline, Rose and Walters (2024), Section IV.B, Figure 2A, and slide 38: the heat map of pairwise posterior probabilities for the first names of KRW’s name analysis (KRW call the posteriors beliefs). Slide 54 shows the same heat map for the firms. KRW put one half on the diagonal by convention; postrank leaves the diagonal empty.

title: Ranking noisy estimates
text: Thirty simulated units are ranked by their estimates, with the largest first. Each estimate is a fixed true value plus sampling error; units with fewer observations have larger standard errors (SEs). Less precise units tend to be overrepresented at both extremes. The initial dataset and twenty repetitions illustrate this effect and its variation between datasets. The true values remain fixed.

title: Ranking noisy estimates
text:
Numerical illustrations

First draw. Of the 10 extreme positions by estimate, small units hold 5, medium units 4 and large units 1 in this draw; by true value they hold 3 small, 4 medium and 3 large units.
True values. In the first draw, of the top 10 by estimate, 9 are in the true top 10 (7.45 on average over the twenty replays). U19, a small unit with true rank 11, is the first of the bottom five: this displacement is due to sampling error. U18, a large unit with true rank 30, sits two rows above them: noisier small and medium units fell past it, and its own estimate came out above its true value.
Twenty replays. The draw menu brings any replay into the table. On average over the 20 replays, small units hold 4.35 of the 10 extreme positions and large units 2.00, and the estimates order 83.90 of the 435 pairs the wrong way, against 88.12 expected over many draws.
Replay 11. The effect varies between repetitions: here small units hold 2, medium units 5 and large units 3, as many large units as by true value. The stated effect concerns average positions across repetitions.
Extremes highlighted. When true values are hidden, the shaded rows do not identify which units have genuinely extreme values. In the replay chart, against the truth, 3 small and 3 large units (dashed line), small units sit above it in most replays and large units on it or below.







Real units have unknown true values, so this check is not possible. The firms of Kline, Rose and Walters (2024), KRW, came with SEs of very different sizes: the race estimates have SEs from .025 to .444 (Section V.B; talk slides 47–49). title: Monte Carlo error in pairwise probabilities
text: Pairwise error probabilities are estimated by the proportion of posterior draws in which a proposed direction is wrong. Independent draws from the six tutorial sites’ normal distribution give estimates and intervals of ±2 Monte Carlo standard errors (MCSE), displayed beside the exact probabilities. More draws reduce numerical uncertainty. A comparison is marked fragile when its interval includes the withholding cost τ. Such isolated-pair sensitivity need not change the optimal coherent report.

title: Monte Carlo error in pairwise probabilities
text:
Numerical illustrations

S 1,000. In this run (seed 1), A–B is estimated .198 against the exact .188, MCSE .0126 (2 MCSE ≈ .0247 with the exact e), so τ .20 makes it fragile. With at most 3 grades A and B share a grade in 100 of the 100 runs: the report changed in 0 of the 18 runs where A–B’s choice flips.
All reports. The report changed in 18 of the 18 runs where A–B’s choice flips; in 5 more runs its estimate equals τ and 2 reports share the smallest risk. The exact report is among the optima in 82 of 100.
S 100. MCSE .0402 in this run (2 MCSE ≈ .0782 with the exact e), radius .1788; the exact .188 stays.
S 4,000. Radius .0283. This run still flags A–B (estimate .203, MCSE .0064): its exact value lies .0116 from τ, inside 2 MCSE (≈ .0124 with the exact e); 54 of 100 runs flag it.
C–D at τ .35. In this run (seed 1) of 400 draws C–D (exact .362) is flagged: estimated .360, MCSE .0240. Its choice flips in 35 runs; the report changed in 0 of the 35 runs with at most 3 grades, in 35 of the 35 runs with any number.
Both scores. At seed 4, E–F’s estimate .202 lands above τ, so the report from the estimates withholds it, unlike the exact report; at seed 1, E–F is fragile at .192 yet stated.







The radius is postrank’s (postrank_iid_bounds(), no ties); the theory book’s form allows ties (4M for 2M). The envelope needs independent whole-state draws and an S fixed before drawing (an effective sample size cannot replace S in it); the MCSE shown is the IID one, as postrank_mc_fragility() computes it for independent draws (for chains it uses an MCMC MCSE). The reruns use consecutive seeds, wrapping from 4,294,967,295 back to 1 at the supported endpoint.

title: Marginal interval overlap and direction probabilities
text: Consider independent normal posterior distributions for A and B with equal standard deviations. The upper figure shows their central credible intervals; the lower figure shows the posterior distribution of the difference A − B. The standard deviation of the difference is √2 times the common posterior SD, whereas the sum of the two marginal SDs is 2 times that quantity. Interval overlap and the probability of a positive difference consequently measure different features of the posterior. A direction can have high posterior probability even when the marginal intervals overlap substantially.

title: Marginal interval overlap and direction probabilities
text:
Numerical illustrations

Just touch, 90%. The intervals meet at 1.645, and the posterior means are 3.290 posterior SDs apart. The difference has SD 1.414, so they are 2.326 of its SDs apart, and A is very probably the higher: .990.
Just touch, 95%. Wider intervals touch only farther apart, at 3.920 posterior SDs, so touching 95% intervals correspond to direction probability .997.
Means 2 SDs apart. The intervals overlap by 1.290 posterior SDs, and the chance that A’s true value is larger is still .921.
Means 1 SD apart. An overlap of 2.290 posterior SDs corresponds to direction probability .760.







When two 90% intervals just touch, A is very probably the higher, .990, for two independent normal posteriors with equal SDs (.997 for 95% intervals). With unequal SDs the distance at which the intervals touch and the SD of the difference change, and the probability with them. Kline, Rose and Walters (2024, section IV.C and Figure 3) draw a credible interval beside each first name, but they grade the names from pairwise posterior probabilities, not from whether the intervals overlap.

title: Posterior dependence and pairwise comparisons
text: For a bivariate normal posterior distribution, the variance of A − B depends on the covariance between the two true values. Positive correlation reduces this variance, whereas negative correlation increases it. The shaded region below the equality line has posterior probability π_AB; the ellipse encloses .90 of the joint posterior probability. Correlation is varied while the marginal distributions and mean difference remain fixed. The resulting probability approaches or recedes from one half, without crossing it. A second specification derives the dependence from uncertainty about a shared prior mean.

title: Posterior dependence and pairwise comparisons
text:
Numerical illustrations

Correlation .50. The ellipse leans along the line: the true values move together, so their difference is less uncertain: SD .200 against .283 if independent, and π_AB = .841 against .760.
Independent. Correlation 0 with equal SDs draws a circle: the difference has SD .283, and π_AB = .760.
Correlation .95. Strong positive dependence gives a difference with SD .063, and π_AB = .999.
Correlation −.95. The ellipse lies across the line, and the difference widens to SD .395: π_AB falls to .694, toward one half, not past it.
Shared prior mean. Estimates .30 and .10 with SEs .20; true values spread with SD .10 around an uncertain prior mean (SD .50). The model gives correlation .645, SD .126 for the difference and π_AB = .624; taken as independent, they would give .212 and .575. With prior-mean SD set to 0, the correlation vanishes, each posterior narrows to SD .089, and π_AB stays .624.







Where the correlation comes from. Given the prior mean, each posterior mean keeps the share k = prior SD²/(prior SD² + SE²) of its estimate, independently. Both posterior variables depend on the uncertain prior mean, so their covariance is (1 − k_A)(1 − k_B)v, with v the prior mean’s variance given both estimates (theory book, ch. 18); with equal SEs the shared part cancels from the difference. postrank takes such posteriors as joint draws, or as normal laws averaged over the prior mean (postrank_mixture_coefficients()).

title: League tables and report cards
text: Kline, Rose and Walters (2024), hereafter KRW, estimated race and gender contact gaps from fictitious applications sent to 97 large U.S. employers. The gaps measure contact advantages for distinctively white over Black names and male over female names. Ranking the estimates states a direction for every firm pair. KRW’s cards state directions between grades only, and these can disagree with the estimate ranking. The displays compare the statements for each firm.

title: League tables and report cards
text:
Numerical illustrations

Race card. The table states a direction for each of the 4,656 pairs of firms. KRW’s race card states 1,324 of them (.284): 1,219 run as the table does and 105 the other way; it is silent on the other 3,332.
Second place. Nationwide is second by estimate (.402 ± .216) but shares grade 2 with 80 other firms. Of its pairs with the other 96 firms, the card states 16: 15 as the table does and 1 the other way, Genuine Parts (sixth by estimate) above it.
Last place. State Farm has the lowest race estimate, −.544, and the largest SE, .444, yet stands at rank 14 by posterior mean (.155), pulled up by KRW’s race prior (normal–normal posterior shrinkage). Of its 16 stated pairs: 2 as the table does and 14 the other way.
By posterior mean. Genuine Parts (Napa Auto) now leads (.250), though sixth by estimate (.330 ± .071). It shares grade 1 with AutoNation, the largest estimate (.433). Now every one of the card’s 1,324 directions runs as the table does.
Gender card. The table now ranks the gender estimates. The card’s four grades, sizes 1, 3, 89, 4, state 731 pairs (.157): 730 run as the table does and 1 the other way. Builders FirstSource is alone in grade 1, so all 96 of its pairs are stated.







Sources: KRW’s Introduction and Section VI, “Racial Discrimination Report Cards” (Figure 7, the race card), Section VIII (Figure 14, the gender card), and talk slides 4–5 and 61–63 (card layout after slides 61–63). On the race card, grade 1 is KRW’s ★ (one star), which KRW call the worst grade. A shared grade means “not compared”, not “equal”. title: Reports from supplied posterior summaries
text: The tool accepts posterior means and standard deviations, estimates and standard errors with a declared prior, or supplied pairwise probabilities. It calculates the implications of those inputs for a coherent grade report and identifies the searched family. normal-summary inputs impose independence across units; probability matrices require explicit event and source declarations. Public examples illustrate these alternatives. Pasted records remain in the component’s memory, and downloads retain the applied input and settings. A URL records settings rather than the pasted records, so reproducing a local-input analysis requires supplying those records again.

title: Reports from supplied posterior summaries
text:
Numerical illustrations

Eight posterior summaries uses the league’s first 8 units, whose precisions differ. Its report states 17 pairs and has weighted risk .1455. The family tag specifies the scope of this optimum.
Eight estimates, flat prior takes each true value as normal around its estimate with its SE. The risk is .1368. The selected grades happen to agree here, although the probabilities and posterior uncertainties differ.
Eight estimates, Normal prior states a prior centred at zero with SD .15. It returns the same posterior as the first example, and risk .1455. An estimate and an SE do not identify that prior by themselves.
Two probability matrices evaluates the supplied two-criterion six-site arrays. The common report states 9 pairs, with weighted risk .0933. The roster has no invented means or intervals.
Thirty posterior summaries exceeds an enumeration limit. The report is best along the weighted expected-rank order: 251 stated pairs and risk .1581. The declared order depends on the criterion weights.
All reports tied has 541 minimising reports. The first 100 are retained and the total remains visible. The all-withheld report has no stated pairs, so its wrong-among-stated share is NA.

For normal inputs, units are treated as independent given the model. Correlated units need joint draws or a joint law in R. Matrix inputs require declarations of the probability event, zero latent equality, zero comparison margin and source. Passing shape, range and reverse-sum checks does not establish a realizable joint law, model calibration or numerical accuracy. Unassessed units remain outside the input; a bottom grade would assert adverse comparisons.
Apply replaces the report only after the input passes its checks. Downloads include the applied input and settings. The URL contains choices and settings, never the pasted records or source descriptions; a local-input analysis therefore requires the records again after reload. The optional joint solver loads only on an explicit action, and its status and gap concern optimisation of the supplied probabilities.
Open the standalone tool.
Related applications: Grade reports as pairwise decisions · The matrix of pairwise posterior probabilities · Computation of optimal grade reports.

title: Report stability under repeated measurement
text: Repeated measurements of the same units yield different estimates, posterior summaries and grade reports. The simulation compares relations between pairs across two such measurements, distinguishing new disclosures, new withholding decisions and reversals. Stability is evaluated alongside disclosure and each report’s expected errors. This is necessary because a rule that always withholds has perfect stability without stating any direction. The true values and standard errors remain fixed, while each dataset receives a newly computed posterior under the specified prior. The experiment therefore concerns repeated-data stability rather than posterior variation at fixed data.

title: Report stability under repeated measurement
text:
Numerical illustrations

Optimal cuts. The first observation states 251 pairs. The second report and relation-change grid show that the criterion is the same, but the measurements and fitted posterior summaries change. The pair control selects a repeated-measurement experiment.
Estimate tiers. The first report states 300 pairs. The fixed tier sizes keep disclosure constant here, even when different units occupy those grades. The comparison table separates disclosure from the fraction of changed relations.
Prior SD .05. The same measurements are reused with a narrower assumed prior. The posterior means, probabilities and optimised cuts are recomputed. This changes the stipulated producer; it does not change the fixed truth or estimate that prior from the observations.
Withhold every pair. Every relation stays withheld. The claimed error fraction reads NA: no disclosure. Its stability is no evidence that the report is informative.
τ .05. A lower price makes withholding cheaper. The histogram and disclosure column describe repeated-data stability, separately from reporting risk.







The simulation fixes the units, true values and SEs, then draws independent normal measurement errors. Both observations get a newly computed posterior under the chosen fixed prior. This is remeasurement at fixed truth, not posterior draws at fixed data or a calibration identity. Each claimed error fraction concerns its own supplied posterior. The pooled claim adds expected wrong counts and divides by total disclosure; it is not an average of the fractions. The optimised rule searches cuts of the declared posterior-mean order, not every possible report.



Standalone: stability, for example ?preset=cuts&pair=2.
Related applications: Fixed quantile tiers, Tiers and optimised cuts of posterior rankings, Averaging error shares across reports.

title: Comparison at matched disclosure
text: Rules that disclose different numbers of pairs need not be comparable by expected wrong count alone. At each rule’s own disclosure, the frontier gives the smallest expected count attained by a report in the family or by a mixture of two complete reports. The vertical difference measures excess expected errors at that disclosure. The display also identifies the best single report when the same count is attainable without randomisation. A rule outside the specified family retains its evaluated risk but receives no frontier comparison within that family.

title: Comparison at matched disclosure
text:
Numerical illustrations

Same N, τ .20. Posterior-mean tiers state 21 pairs with E 3.114. The frontier is 2.951, a gap of .1634. The mixture prints the more-disclosing report with chance .667; the best single report at that N has E 3.013.
Estimate tiers. Three tiers from the estimates also state 21 pairs, but their gap is .6429.
Flags. The flag report states 19 pairs and lies on the frontier: gap 0.
Strict order, τ .05. Stating all 28 pairs leaves a gap of .2305. The cross marks risk above all-withheld at this τ; changing τ does not change this rule’s gap.
At most three grades. Among 6,051 reports, the estimate tiers’ gap becomes .4796. The posterior-mean tiers reach the capped frontier, where only balanced reports with sizes three, three and two attain the endpoint.
Four tiers outside the cap. The rule is outside this family and receives no benchmark. The all-withheld rule remains available in the select, at N 0.







Every rule uses one supplied teaching posterior; postrank does not fit it. The flags use the mean of all thirty league estimates, even on these eight units. A frontier mixture averages complete reports: each realised report states one endpoint’s N. Its error fraction is a ratio of expected counts, not an average of realised fractions. The gap assesses this loss and disclosure, not the purpose for which a rule was designed.









NoteIn postrank





The package’s synthetic pr_example_gaussian poverty example uses its own thirty sites. At τ .25 with at most four grades, this prints quantile cuts with N 337 and risk .1758, versus optimal cuts with N 303 and risk .1603. The risks correspond to different N; H(m) is not a package output.
w <- c(poverty=1, frl=0, snap=0); s <- postrank_settings(weights=w, tau=.25, G_max=4L); sc <- pr_example_gaussian$means[, "poverty"]
sapply(c("quantile", "optimal"), function(r) unlist(postrank_cuts(sc, pr_example_gaussian, s, direction="descending", rule=r)$evaluation[c("N", "primary_risk")]))



Standalone: open this app, for example ?preset=cap3&theme=dark.
Related applications: The error–disclosure frontier · Common withholding cost and matched disclosure.

title: Restrictions imposed by a fixed order
text: In the specified three-unit posterior, A has the largest posterior mean but the largest true value only in the less probable state. Contiguous cuts of the posterior-mean order can consequently exclude a lower-risk grade report. The state table specifies the posterior law, and the complete report table establishes the unrestricted benchmark. The boundary display then identifies the reports excluded by each imposed order. Varying the withholding cost shows where this restriction affects the optimum and where both families select the same report. The comparison concerns this particular law and does not imply a general ranking of ordering methods.

title: Restrictions imposed by a fixed order
text:
Numerical illustrations

Mean order: τ .25. At two stated pairs, the mean-order boundary expects 7/10 wrong directions against 3/10 with any order. Those are expected counts, not risks. At the current price, mean-order cuts withhold everything at risk .2500; the best report puts B above A and C at risk .1833.
Expected ranks: τ .25. The order becomes B, C, A and its best cut recovers risk .1833. The highlighted summary row and report strips follow the order switch; all four rule cards remain available.
Equal risk: τ .30. Reports 2/1/2 and 3/1/2 share the minimum. Both disclosure counts and the equal-risk tolerance are reported because the optimum is not unique.
Mean order: τ .50. The mean-order cuts have risk .4000 against .2000 for the best report. The expected-rank order still reaches the unrestricted boundary.
Mean order: τ .10. Both methods withhold every pair at risk .1000. The imposed order misses only above the cost at which disclosure first becomes worthwhile.







This is one stipulated joint law, not a general failing of posterior-mean orders. The posterior-mean order is not an expected-rank algorithm’s output. Each optimum is conditional on its supplied law, price and feasible family; exact cuts search one order, while the joint benchmark searches every admissible report. Changing the cap changes that comparison. The curve compares methods at each common price and does not compare risks across different prices.



Standalone: order-misses, for example ?order=rank&tau=.25.
Related applications: Tiers and optimised cuts of posterior rankings, Restrictions on the report family.

title: Coherence of pairwise threshold decisions
text: An isolated-pair threshold states a direction when its error probability is strictly below τ and otherwise withholds the pair. Applying this rule independently can produce relations inconsistent with any ordered grade report. In particular, two withheld pairs may require a shared grade that contradicts the stated direction of the third pair. The triple display records these conflicts and strict directed cycles. Superimposing the archived card’s grade blocks identifies the differences between independent threshold decisions and a coherent complete report, using the released probabilities for evaluation.

title: Coherence of pairwise threshold decisions
text:
Numerical illustrations

Race λ .25. Naive thresholding states 1,575 directions. Among 147,440 triples, 32,773 have two pairs withheld and the third stated. For the selected triple, the withheld pairs would force every firm into the same grade, contradicting the stated direction.
Race λ .10. The two-withheld count is 24,278. The triple selector and map arrows locate other conflicts in the matrix.
Race λ .50. The count falls to 15,107. More confident pairs do not make the consistency problem grow monotonically. The curve counts every triple.
Race λ .75. The count falls again to 3,108. The curve distinguishes the different failure types. Absence of strict directed cycles alone cannot establish that the pair choices form a coherent report.
Race λ .25, card blocks. The card withholds 575 confident pairs and states 324 directions whose errors exceed τ. The selected triple retains its identity within these blocks. KRW’s card has no cap on the number of grades, so these differences arise from coherence.
Gender λ 1.00. All 4,656 pairs are stated, but 1 directed cycle precludes a coherent grade report. The absence of cycles at the race baseline does not extend to every target and threshold.







Shared grades withhold directions; they assert neither equality nor indistinguishability of the true values. The threshold counts use the released signed-target pair probabilities. Archived cards were selected with KRW’s code under archived probabilities and are evaluated here under the released law. This is a consistency diagnostic, not a new solve or a certificate that these archived cards minimise postrank’s loss.

Provided as is, without warranty. The data describe KRW’s correspondence experiment, not any firm’s current conduct.



Standalone: naive-thresholding, for example ?lambda=.25&blocks=true&triple=0.
Related applications: Coherence constraints on pairwise decisions, Deciles and quartiles of posterior means.

title: Standardised-evidence flags in a league
text: The standardised-evidence rule assigns three flags to a league of thirty units. Its reference is the mean of the thirty estimates, treated as fixed in the calculation. This treatment is a modelling assumption because the reference is itself estimated. The estimate display and relation matrix identify the directions stated between flag groups, including reversals of the estimate order. Posterior evaluation then gives the expected errors and risk of that fixed report. Changing the posterior or withholding cost changes the evaluation without changing the inputs used to assign the flags.

title: Standardised-evidence flags in a league
text:
Numerical illustrations

League, cutoff 1.96. The flag groups contain 6, 22 and 2 units. They state 188 of 435 pairs. Under the teaching posterior, E/N is .130 and risk is .1696. The grey row bands identify units placed below another unit whose estimate is smaller; the outlined matrix cells locate the same reversals.
Same flags, flat prior. The report still states 188 pairs. Error and risk are reevaluated under independent normal posteriors centred on the estimates, with SDs equal to their SEs. Changing the posterior changes the evaluation without changing the rule’s inputs.
League, cutoff 2.576. The stricter cutoff changes membership of the outer flag groups. The matrix changes in whole blocks: all pairs between different flag groups are stated, and all pairs within a group are withheld. A withheld cell does not assert equality.
Same report, τ .10. The same 188 pairs are stated. The all-withheld comparison has risk τ = .10. The cheaper baseline depends on the withholding cost even when the report does not change.







At the first setting, 20 stated directions run against the estimates. The largest stated error is .649, so an average below the withholding cost does not mean that every individual direction is reliable. These are evaluations of a fixed report under independent normal posteriors; the flag rule does not optimize this loss and uses neither τ nor the posterior. The full matrix follows decreasing estimates on both axes. Arrow-key selection and tables provide the cell values and the complete list of reversals.



Standalone: flags-in-the-league, for example ?crit=1.96&prior=teaching&tau=.10.
Related applications: Grades based on standardised evidence, Posterior summaries in a grade report.

title: Grades based on standardised evidence
text: A standardised-evidence rule compares an estimate with a reference using zᵢ = (θ̂ᵢ − r)/SEᵢ. Here the reference r is zero. Values above the upper cutoff receive the highest flag, values below the lower cutoff receive the lowest, and the remainder receive the middle flag. Interpreting these flags as ordered grades can place a smaller estimate above a larger one, since the classification also depends on sampling precision. The example evaluates the resulting pairwise statement under alternative normal posterior specifications while keeping the flag rule explicit.

title: Grades based on standardised evidence
text:
Numerical illustrations

Two units, flat prior. A has z = 4.00 and B has z = 1.50. The flags state A above B, although B’s estimate is larger. Taking each true value as normal around its estimate, with its SE, gives error probability .686 and risk .6862. The estimate bars and standardised positions display the source of the reversed order.
Same flags, teaching prior. The error falls to .288; the posterior means are .180 for A and .108 for B. The flags stay put: they use estimates and SEs, while the selected posterior prices their stated direction.
B’s SE .15. B reaches z = 2.00. Both units now receive the same flag, so the report states 0 pairs and has risk .2000. A shared grade withholds a direction; it does not assert that the true values are equal.
Cutoff 2.576. The stricter cutoff separates the flags again. The stated direction has error .736. Changing an estimate or SE can change its flag; changing τ affects only the withholding cost.







NoteIn practice



The rule flags a unit above or below the reference when |zᵢ| is more than 1.96, that is, when its difference from the reference is statistically significant at the .05 level.
This constructed comparator follows the postrank theory book, ch. 17 (the Tennessee procedure in ch. 2 uses a related index with other cutoffs).








TipIn postrank





p <- pnorm((.30-.20)/sqrt(.05^2+.20^2))
x <- postrank::postrank_probabilities(array(c(NA,1-p,p,NA),c(2,2,1),dimnames=list(c("A","B"),c("A","B"),"score")), event="directional_error", zero_ties=TRUE, margin=0, source=list(kind="analytic_reference",description="Two-unit example",conditioning="Independent flat-prior normals"), targets=c(score="True value; larger is higher priority"))
postrank::postrank_evaluate(c(A=1L,B=2L),x,weights=c(score=1),tau=.2)[c("N","E_over_N","primary_risk")]

Related applications: Standardised-evidence flags in a league, The decision for an isolated pair.

title: Expected and state-specific reporting loss
text: A report that minimises posterior expected loss need not have the smallest loss in every latent state. The display holds an optimal report and a comparator fixed, then evaluates both on the same complete posterior draws. The probability that the comparator has smaller realised loss and the mean magnitude of the loss difference describe different properties. The finite-state example provides exact probabilities; the simulations additionally show Monte Carlo variation. The optimality comparison requires a common law and loss, and membership of the comparator in the optimised family.

title: Expected and state-specific reporting loss
text:
Numerical illustrations

Inside the family. Among 63 reports with at most two grades, the best has conditional risk .0940; the two posterior-mean tiers have .1046. Yet that common rule wins 57 of these 100 paired draws. Loss magnitudes matter, not just how often a report wins. Below the dashed diagonal the common rule has smaller realised loss.
Outside the family. The comparison retains the two-grade family but uses a three-tier comparator. Its conditional risk .0417 is below .0940. It was excluded from the family optimised here, so the earlier guarantee does not cover it. The law and the optimised family have stayed fixed.
Two-state law. The best report withholds at risk .2500; the expected-rank order has risk .3000. Nevertheless the rule wins with exact probability .700 and wins 65 of these 100 sampled draws. The state table gives exact probabilities and losses; the scatter remains a sample.
A short run. The rule wins 9 of 10 draws, and the paired mean difference is −.00667, favoring it in this finite sample. The exact conditional difference is positive; the paired Monte Carlo SE quantifies numerical sampling variation.
A silent common rule. Its risk is .2000 and its disclosed-error fraction is “NA: no disclosure.” Silence costs τ per pair, so a report that states nothing does not have zero reporting loss.
Identical reports. The summary reads “ties 100”: both reports have the same loss in every drawn state. Draw selection gives the corresponding state, grades and wrong counts.







Total reporting loss includes wrong stated directions and the withholding cost, divided by all pairs. A wrong fraction divides by stated pairs instead. Conditional dominance requires the same law, loss and optimisation family, including comparator membership; it does not establish superiority at every state or under fixed-truth remeasurement. The paired SE measures sampling of the difference, not uncertainty about the supplied model.



Standalone: embed/better-on-average.html, for example ?preset=short&theme=dark.
Related applications: Comparison at matched disclosure and Selection and evaluation using posterior draws, which selects from estimated coefficients.

title: Posterior equality and withholding
text: Posterior probability of exact equality affects the expected loss of a strict direction. Weak-error loss counts an equal pair as an incorrect directional statement. Equality-neutral loss instead assigns no cost to that state. The same joint posterior can therefore give different optimal actions under the two losses. The display evaluates both directions and withholding as the equality probability varies, and identifies the boundaries at which actions have equal expected cost. Sharing a grade remains a withholding decision under either loss; it does not assert that the true values are equal.

title: Posterior equality and withholding
text:
Numerical illustrations

Equality .40, weak loss. Withholding costs .2500; stating A above B costs .5000 and stating the reverse costs .9000. Equality counts against both strict directions. The grey action is minimum-cost even though A is more likely to be above B than below it.
Equality .40, neutral loss. The same law now gives A above B cost .1000 and withholding cost .1500. The difference comes from consequences at equality. Along the equality slider, weak loss changes its minimum-cost action at .150; neutral loss changes at .600 and approximately .867. The open circles mark the boundaries, where competing actions have equal cost.
No equality. Both loss columns agree, and the all-withheld baseline returns to .2500. Under this law the two targets are always distinct, so charging only for distinct states changes nothing.
Equality .90. B above A has neutral cost 0, while withholding costs .0250. This zero cost does not establish strict superiority: the targets can be equal even though a strict reversal is impossible.
Certain equality. Every neutral action costs 0. Here the targets are identical in every state, so the same-grade guard admits only withholding. The raw disclosed-pair count and the distinct mass are different quantities. A strict row has N = 1 but Q = 0: its Errors / Q reads “NA: no distinct mass”. “No disclosure” is reserved for N = 0.







A shared grade withholds a direction and asserts no equality. The probability of exact equality concerns the joint law, rather than equal posterior means or rounded observations. Comparing the two losses compares different decision problems; a smaller neutral risk is not an improvement under weak-error loss. The all-withheld risks coincide only with no equality mass on every positive-weight criterion and a common action family.









TipIn postrank





The opt-in tie-aware route uses postrank_tie_pairwise() and postrank_tie_evaluate() after the law’s targets and equality declarations are supplied. Vignette m4 gives the full constructor. Its field D is the distinct mass called Q_wˢ here, and R0 is the neutral all-withheld baseline. The ordinary route requires tie-free input.



Standalone: embed/ties-and-withholding.html, for example ?preset=neutral.
Related applications: The decision for an isolated pair · Reporting risk and withholding cost · Mixtures of frontier reports.

title: Reported error and reference-law evaluation
text: A reported error share is an expectation under the posterior distribution used to select the report. Evaluation under a separately specified reference law gives another expectation for the same fixed report. The open point shows the realised share of wrong directions at the simulated league’s fixed true values. These quantities need not coincide. The two lower panels distinguish repeated observation of fixed true values from draws of latent values conditional on the selected observations. This distinction is necessary when interpreting apparent agreement between reported and realised error.

title: Reported error and reference-law evaluation
text:
Numerical illustrations

Same conditional laws. The report states 152 pair directions. Both conditional expectations are .0632, while the fixed-truth realised share is .0526. Matching expectations does not make a single realization equal their common value. Individual repeated datasets give realised shares on either side of this expectation.
Narrow prior, five grades. The report claims .140, while the reference expectation for that same report is .115. Their absolute difference is below the largest pair-error gap, .4981. This setting changes the prior, cost and grade cap together. Moving just the prior slider also selects a new report; each setting’s two expectations evaluate that newly selected report under both laws.
Lower cost, two grades. Only 56 pair directions are stated, with claimed share .0254. The two laws still agree. In the grade groups, pairs inside a grade are withheld, and the denominator counts only pairs stated across grades.
One grade, no disclosure. There are 0 stated directions and every share reads “NA: no disclosure.” No wrong directions is different from a defined error share of zero. The posterior-draw wrong count remains zero because this report makes no comparisons.

The lower panels separate two experiments. Observation replays keep all true values fixed, redraw estimates, and choose a new report each time. Posterior draws instead keep the selected observations and report fixed, then vary latent values under the chosen conditional law. The histogram and running average describe that chosen law; adding draws reduces simulation noise without testing whether the law is correct.






This is a deterministic teaching league, not true values sampled from the reference prior. Its design scale does not establish the reference conditional law as the truth. Fixed-truth observation replays therefore do not instantiate chapter 18’s conditional calibration identity. The pair-gap bound compares two model expectations for one fixed report and does not bound its realised share.



Standalone: reported and realised shares, for example ?priorSd=.05.
Related applications: Expected and realised errors among stated directions, Sensitivity to the prior standard deviation.

title: Grade reports as pairwise decisions
text: An ordered grade report determines a decision for every pair of units. Pairs in different grades receive a stated direction; pairs within a grade are withheld. A shared grade makes no assertion of equality between the true values. The grade labels specify order, with highest priority at the top, rather than numerical distances. Reassigning sites among the boxes changes the induced pairwise relation. The accompanying matrix records these changes and the totals of stated and withheld pairs, permitting comparison of reports with different grade sizes and orders.

title: Grade reports as pairwise decisions
text:
Numerical illustrations

A, then B to E, then F. The report states 9 of the 15 pairs and withholds 6, a share stated of .600. Every comparison involving either end is stated; the middle grade withholds its internal pairs. Moving a middle site into an end grade changes the outlined matrix cells.
Three grades of two sites. The same number of grades now states 12 of the 15 pairs and withholds only 3, a share of .800. Each grade withholds its own internal pair. Disclosure depends on the sizes as well as the number of grades.
Four sites: 1/2/2/2. The smaller report states 3 of the 6 pairs, a share of .500. A focused site button accepts a destination grade number. Enter selects the site, arrow keys specify a destination, and a second Enter completes the move. The dashed boxes create a new grade at either end.
Beyond letter order. The report {B, D} > {C, F} > {A, E} still states 12 of the 15 pairs. Any grouping and ordering can be built. The blue and orange transposed cells represent the same unordered pair: each stated pair appears in both triangles, while the pair count includes it once.







These fictional after-school sites are ordered for practice-documentation visits, with no funding consequence. The matrix represents the supplied report without evaluating the accuracy of its directions. Empty grades disappear after a move, preserving the relative order of the occupied boxes.









TipIn postrank





library(postrank)
postrank_evaluate(c(A=1L,B=1L,C=2L,D=2L,E=3L,F=3L), pr_tutorial$one, weights=c(score_A=1), tau=.2)$N # 12
canonical_postrank_grade(c(A=3L,B=3L,C=7L,D=7L,E=9L,F=9L), LETTERS[1:6]) # 1 1 2 2 3 3



Standalone: report builder, for example ?units=6&grades=3,1,2,1,3,2.
Related applications: Reporting risk and withholding cost, Expected errors in a strict ranking.

title: The decision for an isolated pair
text: For an isolated pair, the action with the smallest posterior expected loss depends on the direction probability and the cost of withholding. The two strict directions incur their respective error probabilities; withholding incurs a fixed cost τ. The graph expresses these losses as functions of e_AB = 1 − π_AB, the probability that stating A above B is wrong. An increase in π_AB therefore moves the selected pair to the left. The horizontal withholding line and the two directional lines identify the loss-minimising actions, including ties at their intersections.

title: The decision for an isolated pair
text:
Numerical illustrations

π .85, τ .10. Stating A above B is wrong with probability .15, above the .10 cost of withholding, which minimises loss. The grey dot marks this minimum despite the posterior support for A above B. Its height varies with the withholding cost.
π .85, τ .20. The posterior is unchanged, but the withholding cost increases. The error remains .15, below .20, so the selected action is “state A above B”. Only the horizontal line moved; the posterior probability and both directional costs stayed fixed.
π .80, τ .20. The error equals .20: stating A above B and withholding have equal expected loss, labelled “equally good”. The open circle marks their crossing, and both dots receive a ring. A ring identifies a minimum-cost action at the current pair; it does not identify a correct direction in the unknown truth.
π .50, τ .50. Both directions cost .50 and withholding also costs .50; the summary reads “all three actions are equally good”. The crossing circles merge, while the table marks every action as minimum-cost.

The shaded area follows the smallest cost along the whole error axis. The scale above the graph connects a direction probability to its error, and the table beside it gives the costs at the selected pair.






This example gives equal true values probability zero. For an isolated pair, disclose only when the posterior probability of the direction exceeds 1 − τ; at equality, disclosing and withholding tie. A shared grade withholds a direction rather than asserting equal true values. Combining many pair decisions into one coherent report adds a constraint that this isolated-pair rule does not impose.



Standalone: embed/one-pair.html, for example ?pi=.9&tau=.05 or ?preset=pi80&theme=dark.
Related applications: Pairwise posterior direction probabilities · Grade reports as pairwise decisions · Reporting risk and withholding cost.

title: 2 · From ranks to grades
text:
An ordered grade report states directions between grades and withholds comparisons within grades. The isolated-pair decision defines the relevant action costs, while the report construction example specifies the relations induced by complete grade assignments. Posterior reporting risk combines expected wrong directions and withholding cost. The remaining applications examine coherence, the error–disclosure frontier, report-family restrictions and alternative error summaries. This framework also permits evaluation of the common rules considered in Part 3.





2.1

title: The error–disclosure frontier
text: Each point represents a report, with its number of stated pairs on the horizontal axis and expected wrong count on the vertical axis. A supporting line of slope τ identifies a report with minimum posterior risk in the selected family. The lower convex boundary summarises these choices across withholding costs. Its vertices are attained by reports; points within its edges may require mixtures of complete reports. The display distinguishes this convex boundary from the minimum error attainable by a single report at each discrete disclosure level.

title: The error–disclosure frontier
text:
Numerical illustrations

τ .20, all reports. The touched vertex states 14 pairs and expects .3576 wrong directions, with risk .0372. The vertex table records this report and its adjacent slopes. The circles below the grey columns mark the smallest error at each attainable disclosure; only some of those circles are corners of the dashed boundary.
τ .15, all reports. A lower withholding cost selects a smaller disclosure: 13 pairs, .1692 expected wrong directions and risk .0313. The posterior did not change. The smaller slope reduces the loss reduction available from additional disclosure.
τ .40, all reports. The line reaches the last vertex: 15 stated pairs, .7194 expected wrong directions and risk .0480. This is the strict order. The Every report (full height) view gives the full vertical range; the close view resolves reports near the frontier.
τ .20, at most 3 grades. Only 603 reports are available. The boundary ends at 12 stated pairs and .02477 expected wrong directions; the selected report has risk .0417. The missing corners belong to reports outside this family, so they cannot be selected even when withholding becomes costly.

The table’s edge slopes are the withholding costs where the selected report changes. They are also the change points in The withholding cost: each measures the extra expected wrong directions per extra stated pair. When the line lies along an edge, both endpoint reports have the same risk.






The dashed segments describe mixtures of complete reports, so a point between corners need not be a deterministic report. These are fictional tutorial sites under one supplied posterior and one criterion. KRW’s related empirical figure is Figure 6 in Section V.E, “Reporting Possibilities”; the cloud here is computed from the tutorial law.









TipIn postrank





library(postrank)
p <- postrank_frontier(pr_tutorial$one, weights=c(score_A=1), tau=c(.15,.20,.40), G_max=6L, backend="highs")
p$table[, c("tau", "N", "primary_risk")]
This returns selected reports along a withholding-cost path. It does not compute the convex boundary or the mixtures between its vertices.



Standalone: embed/frontier.html, for example ?tau=.15&family=all&view=near.
Related applications: Reporting risk and withholding cost · The decision for an isolated pair · Posterior summaries in a grade report.

title: Restrictions on the report family
text: An optimum is defined relative to a specified family of reports. A grade cap, an exact number of occupied grades and contiguous cuts of a declared order impose different restrictions. The rows compare each family’s minimum risk at a common withholding cost and on a common scale. Reordering the units changes the fixed-order family, while leaving the unrestricted family unchanged. The examples identify when a restricted optimum coincides with the unrestricted optimum and when the restriction raises risk. Each result is accompanied by the family over which it was obtained.

title: Restrictions on the report family
text:
Numerical illustrations

Exactly six. The family contains 720 strict rankings. Its best report costs .0480, while the unrestricted reference costs .0372. Requiring every site to have its own grade forces the report to state an uncertain direction. The selected row identifies this direction and its error probability.
At most three. The capped family contains 603 reports, including reports that use fewer grades. Exactly the required number gives a smaller family of 540. Here both best risks are .0417; the shared scale makes that equality visible. Further grade restrictions can change the minimum at this fixed cost.
B before A. The declared order allows 32 contiguous reports. Its best cut costs .0379, above the unrestricted .0372. The unit arrows modify the declared order. The dynamic program searches cuts of the declared order, and the row checks its answer against enumeration of those same cuts.
Two criteria. The four-unit example has 24 reports with every grade distinct, 75 in the unrestricted family, and 8 contiguous cuts. The exact-count row costs 7/40. The law’s table gives the criterion-specific errors and their weighted average: the orange segment now measures expected weighted wrong directions.
A dominating set. At τ = 4/9, every unrestricted best report separates {A, B} above {X, Y}, at risk 4/15. The best report with the grade cap costs 17/54 and puts X with A. The cap can make the separating rearrangement infeasible. The law panel checks the strict cross-set premise again whenever you change the price.







Every optimum belongs to a declared family. Enlarging a family cannot increase its smallest risk at a fixed price, but changing the price changes the decision problem. The dashed mark is the all-withheld risk; an exact-count family need not contain that report. Equal-risk reports are identified in the rows, and the order family states its tie rule. All examples are specified for teaching.









TipIn postrank





library(postrank)
sc <- postrank_expected_rank(pr_tutorial$one)
postrank_cuts(sc, pr_tutorial$one, postrank_settings(weights=c(score_A=1), tau=.2, G_max=6L, exact_G=6L), rule="optimal")$risk
This cuts the expected-rank order; its result agrees with the exact-count optimum here.

title: Computation of optimal grade reports
text: Selection of a minimum-risk grade report requires both a report family and an optimisation method. Candidate counts describe the size of the family; the binary relation describes the coherence constraints. Dynamic programming optimises contiguous cuts of a specified order, while a joint solver can search across orders. The displays connect these formulations and identify the scope of each result. Solver outputs include the incumbent risk, a lower bound and the absolute risk gap. Agreement between methods on an example does not extend the scope of a restricted search.

title: Computation of optimal grade reports
text:
Numerical illustrations

DP: six sites, τ .20. The posterior-mean order admits 16 contiguous reports with at most three grades. Its current answer is {A, B} > {C, D} > {E, F}, with risk .0417. Enumeration checks all 603 reports in the capped family and finds the same answer here. The agreement is specific to these inputs.
DP: inspect one cell. The table has filled 8 of 15 feasible cells. For the current cell’s alternatives, the last cut is at b = 2. “Next cell” advances the recursion; “Fill table” shows the backtrack. The selected report remains visible above the recursion controls. Negative savings mean withholding costs more than stating those fixed-order directions.
Twelve units. The unrestricted family contains 28,091,567,595 reports. At most three grades reduces that to 523,251, while a declared order permits only 67 contiguous cuts. Equal vertical distances on the log axis represent multiplication.
A broken binary pattern. The pattern is not transitive, though completeness holds: 2 > 1. No grade vector produces this relation. The valid-pattern view enumerates all thirteen coherent reports; setting both directions to one means a shared grade, not latent equality.
Joint search: twenty units. HiGHS loads only when the joint-search control is activated for 20 league units. The output gives the status, incumbent risk, lower bound and absolute risk gap. The separate four-unit example has risks .1750 and .1500 under different grade-count restrictions, showing why a bound must keep its family.







The six fictional sites use the postrank tutorial’s score-A normal posteriors. The solver uses a frozen simulated league with independent normal posteriors; its objective includes the constant offset, so R = τ + Z/M and a raw objective gap is divided by M. A relative objective gap is not a risk gap. A solver status or zero gap does not certify exact arithmetic or the posterior model. These distinctions follow theory chapter 14 and vignette m5. The R package selects HiGHS explicitly; Gurobi is its default backend and there is no automatic fallback.









TipIn postrank





library(postrank)
g <- c(A=1L,B=1L,C=2L,D=2L,E=3L,F=3L)
postrank_evaluate(g, pr_tutorial$one, weights=c(score_A=1), tau=.2)$primary_risk
This evaluates the displayed three-grade report directly, without invoking a solver.

title: Coherence in a finite three-unit example
text: A finite posterior assigns probability to four possible orders of A, B and C. For some withholding costs, the individually optimal pair decisions cannot be represented by any ordered grade report. Evaluating all 13 reports establishes the minimum coherent risk and the additional cost relative to the separate pairwise decisions. Each bar separates the contribution of expected wrong directions from the contribution of withheld pairs. Because the posterior has finite support, these quantities are calculated exactly, without Monte Carlo estimation. Changes in τ alter the relative action costs while the posterior probabilities remain fixed.

title: Coherence in a finite three-unit example
text:
Numerical illustrations

τ .20. The pairwise choices cost 1/6 per pair, but the optimal coherent reports cost 11/60. Each states an extra direction with error 1/4. The two reports beneath the bars identify the additional directions and their error probabilities. The dashed line is a lower bound, attained by no report at this setting.
τ .10. Giving everyone the same grade, {A, B, C}, costs 1/10. The outer pair can now be stated or withheld at equal cost. Some set of the minimum-cost pairwise actions is coherent, and the best bar reaches the dashed line.
τ .25. There are 3 equally good reports, all at risk 1/5. Their orange and grey segments show that the same total risk can combine different amounts of disclosure and withholding. The text retains every equal-risk optimum.
τ .30. The full order {A} > {B} > {C} has risk 1/5. Raising the withholding cost changes the choice without changing the posterior law. Keyboard selection provides each report’s risk, disclosure and directions with error above the current withholding cost.







The law is set by hand for teaching, from the theory book’s three-unit example. Each bar is one complete report: its first segment is expected wrong directions per pair, and its second pays for withheld pairs. Grades decide all pairs together, so a direction with error above the price can appear in a best report. That is compatible with the report’s overall optimality. Exact fractions make the comparison inspectable; no draws or simulation error enter these calculations.









TipIn postrank





The package evaluates both fixed reports under these directional errors; it does not search for them. Each returns risk 11/60 at τ = 1/5. The input records the same finite teaching law used above.
e <- matrix(c(NA,1/4,1/10,3/4,NA,1/4,9/10,3/4,NA),3,byrow=TRUE,dimnames=rep(list(c("A","B","C")),2))
input <- postrank::postrank_probabilities(e,criterion="priority",event="directional_error",zero_ties=TRUE,margin=0,source=list(kind="analytic_reference",description="ABC/ACB/BAC/CBA with masses .60/.15/.15/.10",conditioning="Complete fixed finite target law"),targets=c(priority="Fictional priority; larger is higher"))
vapply(list(c(A=1,B=1,C=2),c(A=1,B=2,C=2)),function(g) postrank::postrank_evaluate(g,input,weights=c(priority=1),tau=1/5)$primary_risk,numeric(1))

title: Averaging error shares across reports
text: When disclosure varies across outcomes, several averages of error shares are possible. The ratio of expected wrong and stated counts weights outcomes in proportion to disclosure. The mean of the defined report fractions instead conditions on positive disclosure and weights those outcomes by their probabilities. Assigning zero to outcomes with no disclosure yields a third quantity. The examples calculate all three from common counts and probabilities, including a randomisation over complete reports and a repeated-dataset simulation. Their differences follow from their denominators and the treatment of outcomes with no stated direction.

title: Averaging error shares across reports
text:
Numerical illustrations

Three outcomes. Pooled pairs give 2/5, the mean among disclosing outcomes is 1/2, and zero-imputation gives 1/3. The chance of disclosure is 2/3 and mean disclosure is 5/9. Changes to wrong and stated counts affect these summaries differently because their denominators differ. The silent outcome has an undefined fraction.
More weight on errors. Giving the error-heavy outcome more probability changes the pooled ratio to 4/7, the disclosing mean to 2/3 and the zero-imputed mean to 1/2. Relative weights are normalised; they describe the distribution over outcomes, rather than extra units inside an outcome.
A complete-report lottery. The four-unit example mixes entire reports. Pooled expected counts give 1/8, while the mean report fraction is 49/400. The lottery probability weights each complete report and its disclosure. Expected weighted errors are averaged within a report before the reporting lottery is applied.
All silent. Both ratio-based summaries read “NA: no disclosure”; the zero-imputed mean is 0. That zero is a convention, not evidence that a disclosed direction was accurate. The probability of any disclosure is reported separately.
Twenty datasets. A simulated league gives pooled error .0892 and a disclosing mean .0891. The running curves and individual counts describe the averages over the selected number of datasets. The true values stay fixed while each dataset produces fresh estimates and its own graded report.







A ratio estimated from a small sample need not be unbiased for a ratio of expectations. The hand-set outcomes provide an exact single-observation example; one trajectory of simulated datasets shows variability, rather than measuring that bias. Simple rational values use fractions in the finite examples; simulated shares use the site’s decimal format.









TipIn R





A <- c(2, 0, 0); N <- c(2, 3, 0)
c(pooled=sum(A)/sum(N), disclosing=mean((A/N)[N>0]), zero_imputed=mean(ifelse(N>0,A/N,0)))

title: Minimising the largest criterion risk
text: Weighted-risk selection minimises an average of expected criterion risks. Deterministic minimax selection instead minimises their largest value. For two criteria, each report’s risk line connects its criterion-specific risks; the weighted rule selects the lowest line at the specified weight, whereas minimax selects the report with the smallest higher endpoint. Both calculations use the same posterior law, withholding cost and feasible report family. The examples also compare deterministic minimax risk with the maximum of the weighted lower envelope, quantities that need not coincide in a restricted discrete family.

title: Minimising the largest criterion risk
text:
Numerical illustrations

w .90. The weighted best averages .0605 but reaches .2296 when only score B counts. At w .70, its weighted risk is .0882 and its worse endpoint is .1378. The price panel compares each selected guarded report with the weighted best under that same loss.
w .30. Both rules choose {A, B, C, D} > {E, F}; its larger expected criterion risk is .0944. The envelope peak panel distinguishes the risk value from the weight where that peak occurs.
Score B only. Two weighted reports share the smallest risk. Their worst endpoint risks are .1996 and .2113; both identities, dashed alternative and complete criterion profiles remain visible.
Book low and Book high. In the restated two-unit law, the weighted rule changes from withholding at risk .2500 to stating A above B at risk .1500. The visible table shows every eligible report’s two criterion risks and their maximum.
Book minimax. The guarded rule continues to withhold, with maximum .2500. Under Zero error weight, the same .2500 guard remains because a zero error weight does not remove a guarded criterion.
Certain opposition. Exactly two grades exclude withholding. The highest point of the lower envelope is .5000, while deterministic minimax is 1.0000. This makes the gap between those two quantities visible.







Note



Minimax here minimises the maximum of expected criterion risks. It does not minimise the expected maximum of realised losses. Grey full lines stay within the displayed vertical range; highlighted lines are clipped, and the keyboard and hidden table retain every eligible report. A shared grade withholds a direction rather than asserting equality. Changing the weight changes the loss, so risks at different weights are not compared as one objective.

The package’s synthetic minimax example also withholds every pair; it uses its own units.

source(system.file("scripts", "_vignette-setup.R", package="postrank", mustWork=TRUE), local=TRUE)
