title: Optimal reports along the criterion-weight path
text: With two criteria, the risk of a fixed report varies affinely with the error weight. The lower envelope identifies the report or reports with minimum weighted risk at each weight, including the common withholding charge. The path is calculated from these functions rather than inferred from a sampled slider grid. Step charts record the criterion-specific expected wrong shares and disclosure, while the risk lines explain the change points. Each interval retains a fixed report, although its weighted risk continues to vary. Boundary solutions are evaluated separately where several reports may be optimal.

title: Optimal reports along the criterion-weight path
text:
Numerical illustrations

Equal weights. The selected report states 9 pairs. Its expected wrong shares are .0177 on score A and .0267 on score B. The interval table and lower envelope identify the weights for which this report is optimal.
Lower A weight. The best report states 12 pairs and favours score B’s ordering of the conflicting sites. Both criterion shares stay constant through the interior of its interval, although the weighted risk changes.
Higher A weight. The report again states 12 pairs, with {A, B} > {C, D} > {E, F}. Its expected wrong share on score B is .237. Equal disclosure does not mean equal pair relations.
Score B only. At the endpoint, 2 reports share the smallest risk. The expected wrong shares on score A are .200 and .215. The boundary table keeps their identities and differing profiles, including the tiny first interval.
No cap. The unrestricted calculation searches all 4,683 reports. The current equal-weight report still states 9 pairs, but the complete path can differ away from the selected weight.
Higher withholding cost. The uncapped current report states 14 pairs. The interval table retains every short interval; both criterion-share paths use these same boundaries.







Note



The path uses the six fictional sites’ declared independent normal posteriors. Each exact boundary can have several best reports; the table solves the boundary itself and states the equal-risk tolerance. A zero-width endpoint entry and a tiny positive interval remain visible in the table even when a screen cannot give them a visible width. Risks at different weights correspond to different losses, so a falling line is not an improvement under one fixed objective. The largest lower-envelope risk is a risk value, while its location is a weight.

title: Posterior profiles on multiple criteria
text: The same units can have different posterior orderings on different criteria. Each panel retains its criterion’s measurement scale, posterior means and marginal intervals. Connecting lines identify units across the separate orders, and the pair display gives the error probability of a proposed direction on each criterion. Aligning rows by unit makes their profiles comparable without constructing a composite score. The examples distinguish opposition between preferred directions from uncertainty within a criterion, and show the effect of reversing the substantive orientation of one target.

title: Posterior profiles on multiple criteria
text:
Numerical illustrations

Thirty sites. There are 397 opposing pairs among 435 pairs. The highest posterior mean belongs to a different site on each criterion. Alignment by unit labels displays each unit’s criterion-specific profiles.
Six sites, B–C. The error of stating B above C is .007 on score A and .961 on score B. The complete list has 3 opposing pairs. A very likely direction on one criterion can be very unlikely on another.
Six sites, B–D. The errors are .002 on score A and .760 on score B. Matching row labels leaves each criterion’s scale intact; it does not turn the scores into one composite.
Reverse score B. Lower score B now means higher priority. The error of stating B above C on the oriented score becomes .039. The supplied information stays the same; the substantive direction of the target changes.
Wider intervals. The marginal level becomes 95%, while the 397 opposing pairs stay the same. Interval level changes the displayed uncertainty bands, not the supplied posterior probabilities or mean orders.







For the fictional six sites, score A is standardised reading growth and score B a standardised family-engagement index; higher values mean higher visit priority by default. Grades would decide only the order of practice-documentation visits, with no funding consequence. These are supplied synthetic normal laws: intervals are marginal, not simultaneous, and thirty-site marginal releases do not supply a composite or sampled joint state.

title: Criterion-specific expected-error budgets
text: An error weight determines the contribution of a wrong direction to risk. An error budget instead restricts its expected share among stated directions on a specified criterion. The cloud plots allowed reports with positive disclosure according to their two criterion-specific error shares. Applying one or both budgets reduces the feasible family. The selected report minimises weighted risk over this remaining family, and is compared with the unconstrained optimum under the same settings. Count-form checks also cover the all-withheld report when it is allowed, despite its undefined error share.

title: Criterion-specific expected-error budgets
text:
Numerical illustrations

Loose budget. With equal weights and score B’s budget at .03, only 3 reports qualify. The best still states 9 of 15 pairs and has risk .0933: removing reports need not change the optimum.
Tight budget. At .02, 2 reports qualify. The best states 8 of 15 pairs and has risk .0939; the other report withholds every comparison. The ring marks the optimum in the reduced family.
Exactly three. Keeping the .02 budget while requiring exactly three grades leaves 0 reports feasible. The empty family has no best report. Relaxing the grade count restores the all-withheld option.
Both budgets. Requiring an expected wrong share at most .02 on each score also leaves 2 reports. Both count-form checks and their slacks are reported; a report must pass both rows.
Zero weight. Score B has zero error weight but still has its .10 budget. The best feasible report has risk .0906. Its largest single score-B error is .240, for E above F, while its average is .0267. A budget on an average allows some individual errors above it.
No budget. The score-A-only best has risk .0417 and expected wrong share .237 on score B. The cross marks this unconstrained best; the older At most .15, At most .10 and At most .05 presets retain the same score-A-only comparison.







These are six fictional sites with independent normal posteriors supplied for illustration. The guarantee is an expectation under that posterior, not the realised share of wrong directions. All-withheld has zero expected wrong count and zero stated pairs: it meets count-form budgets when allowed, although its wrong share is undefined. Changing weights or τ changes the loss; changing the grade cap changes the family. The browser enumerates the six-site reports directly. postrank’s typed-coefficient interface does not accept these budget settings.

title: A random-criterion representation of weighted risk
text: Weighted risk has a random-criterion representation. One auxiliary criterion is selected for the entire fixed report, with selection probabilities equal to the error weights. Averaging its criterion-specific reporting risk gives the same weighted risk as the direct calculation. The selected criterion applies to all units and reported pairs, preserving its within-criterion joint law. This construction averages losses rather than target magnitudes. The report is chosen before the auxiliary criterion is revealed; the representation does not describe a distribution of stakeholder preferences or criterion-dependent report selection.

title: A random-criterion representation of weighted risk
text:
Numerical illustrations

Weighted report. Both calculations give risk .0933. The criterion contributions are .0453 and .0480. Changing the auxiliary criterion changes the evaluated column: the whole outlined column changes, while report 1/1/1/1/2/3 stays fixed.
Certain opposition. The two directions each cost .5000, while withholding costs .3000. Both criteria distinguish the units with certainty. The same criterion choice applies to both units and every reported pair.
Three actions tie. All 3 actions cost .5000. Other retained optima have different criterion-specific risks but the same weighted average. These are different reports, not different reports chosen after the auxiliary criterion is revealed.
Two against one. The cheaper direction costs .3333, the reverse .6667, and withholding .4000. A certain two-against-one split can favor disclosure. The adjacent one-third boundary preset retains both actions sharing the minimum instead of treating equality as a strict preference.
Zero error weight. The cheaper weighted direction costs .0000, although the ignored criterion’s own risk is 1.0000. Its selection chance is 0, so this branch contributes nothing. The vector can still be inspected without pretending the mixture would draw it.
No-cap coherence. Among all 4,683 reports, 1/2/2/3/4/5 states 14 pairs with risk .1275. It states A above C with weighted error .3803 and B above D with .3813, both above τ .35. There is no grade cap in this example.







The report is selected before the auxiliary criterion; conditional on the supplied information, this auxiliary choice is independent of the target law. The mixture retains a whole within-criterion vector law, including unit dependence. Postrank’s weak-error identity allows latent equality. The correspondence to KRW’s strict-count objective additionally requires the same law, targets, orientation, units and feasible family, plus its affine and equality conditions.









TipIn postrank





The fixed default report reproduces the two calculations; small floating-point rounding differences do not change their algebraic identity.

ev <- postrank_evaluate(c(A=1L,B=1L,C=1L,D=1L,E=2L,F=3L), pr_tutorial$two, weights=c(score_A=.5,score_B=.5), tau=.2)
sum(c(.5,.5)*ev$criterion_risk); ev$weighted_risk

title: Composite targets and criterion directions
text: Directional reporting on separate criteria and reporting on a weighted composite define different targets. Error weights determine the cost of criterion-specific mistakes; composite coefficients combine target magnitudes. At the known state A = (1, −2), B = (0, 0), the lower-cost criterion direction can therefore oppose the direction of an equally weighted composite. Both displays use a common withholding cost and report family. Cross-evaluation of the selected reports distinguishes the consequences of the two objectives, including changes induced by rescaling a criterion or transforming the complete finite law.

title: Composite targets and criterion directions
text:
Numerical illustrations

Different targets. The criterion-direction costs are .2500, .7500 and .3000 for forward, reverse and withholding. The composite costs are 1.0000, .0000 and .3000. One objective picks 1/2; the other picks 2/1.
Rescale the second criterion. The composite value of A becomes .250 and its preferred direction flips. The criterion-direction cost .2500 stays the same. The positive multiplier applies to every unit, while error weights and composite coefficients keep their separate roles.
Composite equality. Both strict composite directions cost 1.0000. Withholding costs .3000. Each criterion still distinguishes the units, but their composite is equal; a shared grade withholds rather than asserting that equality.
Two reports, same disclosure. Every one of the 75 reports is evaluated. Criterion directions choose 1/2/2/3 with risk .1417; the composite chooses 1/1/2/3 with risk .0333. Both disclose 5 pairs. Both columns evaluate each selected report under the two objectives.
Transform the whole law. Exponentiating every finite input preserves the criterion best report and its risk .1417. The composite now selects 1/1/2/2 with risk .0667. The complete criterion best-report sets before and after remain visible under the same settings.
Rescale the Normal composite. The first composite mean is .635. This analytic calculation uses the six sites’ declared independence across units and criteria; marginal means alone would not specify its uncertainty.







All examples are synthetic supplied laws. Composite coefficients stay nonnegative and sum to one, matching the package interface. A positive multiplier changes composite magnitudes; a strictly increasing finite-state transformation preserves criterion directions without refitting the law. The two risk scales do not choose the substantive target. No thirty-site joint law is inferred from marginal releases.









TipIn postrank





This prints composite scores of posterior means; weights are composite coefficients. Package scales divide, so a second-criterion scale of ten corresponds to the browser’s multiplier .1.
library(postrank)
postrank_composite(pr_tutorial$law$means, weights=c(score_A=.5,score_B=.5), scales=c(score_A=1,score_B=10))

title: Sensitivity to costs, weights and grade restrictions
text: Withholding costs and error weights specify the reporting loss. A grade cap specifies the feasible family. The exact path varies the withholding cost while holding the posterior, weights and family fixed. A separate grid evaluates every combination of the declared costs, caps and weights. These displays distinguish changes in the objective from changes in admissible reports. Criterion profiles and disclosure describe the consequences without assuming that risks under different losses are directly comparable. The archived examples retain their recorded settings and provide discrete sensitivity comparisons rather than continuous change points.

title: Sensitivity to costs, weights and grade restrictions
text:
Numerical illustrations

Equal weights. The best report states 9 of 15 pairs. Its wrong shares are .0177 and .0267 on scores A and B. The exact path gives its interval and all returned equal-risk alternatives at the boundary costs.
A higher price. The report states 11 pairs; score B’s wrong share is .115. A larger withholding cost can favour additional statements, even though some statements are less certain.
A still higher price. The report states 12 pairs, while score B’s wrong share falls to .0575. Disclosure cannot fall along this fixed-family exact path; a criterion-specific wrong share can move either way.
At most two grades. The best report states 8 pairs with risk .0939. The table that changes only the cap keeps the same price and weights, making its risks comparable; the smallest risk cannot rise as the family expands.
Thirty-site archive. Recorded disclosures include 131, 276, 305 and 312 pairs. These dots describe the saved solves at their recorded prices. Their spacing does not locate the exact transitions of a continuous path.
Tutorial archive. The package’s prepared sensitivity analysis has 7 settings, changing one setting at a time. The live view instead evaluates the full Cartesian grid with a fixed reference grade.







Every row’s comparison reevaluates the same reference grade under that row’s loss. A reference excluded by a cap remains a fixed-report comparator; it does not become an admissible solution. Across changed prices or weights, risk values measure different losses. The thirty-site archives use joint draws and fixed settings, separately from the Gaussian marginal example. Intervals and boundary tables belong to the live exact path; archived dots carry their saved statuses and gaps. The R block below reads the prepared one-at-a-time tutorial archive.

library(postrank)
s <- readRDS(system.file("extdata/cached/tutorial_sensitivity.rds", package="postrank", mustWork=TRUE))$value
s$table[, c("setting_id", "risk", "N")]

title: KRW’s reward and postrank’s withholding cost
text: KRW’s reporting objective rewards a correct direction by λ, charges one for a wrong direction, and assigns zero payoff to withholding. postrank charges one for a wrong direction and τ for withholding. Under the corresponding conversion, the objectives select the same reports when the posterior, target orientation, units and feasible family are common and the target is tie-free. The displays compare the three isolated-pair actions and coherent reports for six sites. A separate audience-model interpretation records the additional behavioural assumptions associated with KRW’s scale.

title: KRW’s reward and postrank’s withholding cost
text:
Numerical illustrations

λ .25 (KRW’s card) gives τ .20 and a direction-probability cut of .80. For a pair on its own, both rules state a direction beyond that cut. Both choose {A} > {B} > {C, D} > {E} > {F} among the six-site reports.
λ .08 gives τ .0741. The audience-share row explains the behavioural interpretation of withholding.
λ .10 gives τ 1/11 and cut 10/11. The best report is {A, B} > {C, D} > {E, F}; a shared grade leaves its units uncompared.
λ .50 gives τ 1/3 and cut 2/3. The dashed and solid lines give the reverse- and forward-direction costs, respectively.
λ 1 gives τ .50 and {A} > {B} > {C} > {D} > {E} > {F}. The two direction cuts meet, and the stipulated informed-audience share reaches zero.
τ .40 works from the other scale: λ is 2/3. The three outcome rows give the payoff and cost transformations.

The correspondence requires one tie-free target, the same posterior probabilities, orientation, units and report family. It is a change of scale under those conditions, not evidence that a posterior is calibrated. Resolving transitivity across many pairs can raise the certainty a single pair needs; an isolated cut is not a separate ceiling on every direction in a coherent report. The audience share is KRW’s stipulated behavioural model, not an estimated share of actual readers.

title: KRW’s archived reward path
text: KRW’s reward parameter λ changes the relative value of correct and incorrect directions. The archived grid contains a card at each hundredth from zero to one. Larger rewards generally correspond to greater disclosure, although individual archived changes need not be monotone. Each fixed card is evaluated using the released pair probabilities. The displays record grade counts, stated pairs, error rates and changes relative to the preceding grid row. The archived selection probabilities and solver tolerances remain relevant when interpreting deviations from properties of an exact optimal path under a single law.

title: KRW’s archived reward path
text:
Numerical illustrations

λ .25: published race card. The baseline card states 1,324 pairs, with E/N .136. Grade counts use a logarithmic scale; DR divides expected errors by every possible pair, separately from the disclosure share.
λ .08: first race split. Genuine Parts stands alone above the other 96 firms. Its standard error is smaller than AutoNation’s, despite AutoNation’s larger estimate. Risk .07406 is just below its own all-withheld reference; the comparison needs the extra decimal.
λ .01: one grade. The first positive λ states no direction. E/N is undefined. The complete table also retains the archived λ-zero endpoint, where postrank risk is unavailable rather than assigned a value.
λ .30: statements and silence. Against the preceding grid row, 830 pairs become stated and 92 become withheld. This comparison always uses neighbouring grid rows, irrespective of your previous slider position.
λ .98: disclosure dip. Between λ .97 and .98, disclosure falls from 4,620 to 4,614. More reward does not justify a claim that every archived step discloses more.
λ 1: end of grid. DR and E/N coincide at .268 because every pair is stated. The complete Purples matrix uses a different scale: it shades stated errors, unlike the Blues direction probabilities in the heat-map app.







Grid cards were computed with KRW’s code under archived probabilities and solver tolerances. Their evaluations here use the released postrank probabilities and supply no new optimality certificate. Race’s baseline card is Figure 7; gender is Figure 14 (§VIII). Figures 5A and 6 are in §V.E, and Figure 10A is in §VI.B.

title: KRW’s race and gender report cards
text: KRW’s report cards state directions between grades and withhold comparisons within grades. Grade 1 denotes the end with the highest oriented target. Race and signed gender gaps have separate target definitions and pairwise posterior probabilities. The cards display firm-level means and intervals together with the error probabilities of stated comparisons. A correct direction receives reward λ, a wrong direction costs 1 and withholding has payoff 0; λ .25 corresponds to τ .20. The discordance rate DR divides the expected wrong count by all 4,656 unordered pairs, whereas E/N uses only stated pairs.

title: KRW’s race and gender report cards
text:
Numerical illustrations

Published race card. The card states 1,324 of 4,656 pairs, with expected wrong share E/N .136. Its risk .1818 splits into .0387 for errors and .1431 for withholding. The full firm display and between-grade table show that directions between distant grades are more reliable than adjacent ones here.
Reveal grade 1. Grades can be displayed sequentially. The remaining bands stay in place; unrevealed firms are omitted from the disclosure and between-grade tables until those grades are displayed.
Sort by estimate. State Farm moves 69 rows inside its grade. Changing the row order changes no reported direction. Genuine Parts and AutoNation illustrate why estimates alone do not determine the card.
λ .08: first race split. The risk .07406 is slightly below all withheld, .07407. The extra decimal prevents rounding from hiding that distinction. The displayed card is still an archived KRW grid card.
Published gender card. It states 731 pairs. Both ends of its signed scale are contact gaps; three stated directions are more likely wrong than right. The note identifies these firms and probabilities.
One grade. Nothing is stated. E/N is NA: no disclosure, meaning undefined; the app draws no E/N bar.

The precision view plots each firm’s original sampling SE against its current grade, with a complete named table. KRW’s prior depends on precision; uncertain firms sharing the middle grade is not evidence of average behavior.






Grid cards were computed with KRW’s code under archived probabilities and solver tolerances. Their evaluations here use the released postrank probabilities and supply no new optimality certificate. Race’s baseline card is Figure 7; gender is Figure 14 (§VIII). Figures 5A and 6 are in §V.E, and Figure 10A is in §VI.B.

title: A high-probability school comparison withheld
text: Schools F and I share a grade in the three-grade optimum, although F above I has high posterior probability. Requiring a specified direction and reoptimising the complete report measures its additional risk within the same family. That difference includes the effects on all other stated and withheld comparisons. The tertiles and a fixed-order four-grade comparison provide further reports that state the direction. Their results identify the roles of the particular grouping and search restrictions without assigning an exclusive cause to the withheld pair.

title: A high-probability school comparison withheld
text:
Numerical illustrations

F above I shows direction probability .9999. Of 175,099 three-grade reports that state it, the least-risk one has risk .064087, slightly above the overall optimum .063774.
I above F reverses the required statement. The best report stating this direction has risk .112261; the posterior probability alone does not summarize its full-report cost.
The tertiles state it uses the two tertile cuts. This fixed report states 48 pairs with risk .082255, so stating F above I does not require a fourth grade.
The higher-cost optimum sets τ to .45. The optimum itself now states F above I and has risk .143197.

The table ranks the three best reports in the same three-grade family. The report stating F above I is second, while the next displayed report is third. The input check excludes self-comparisons.
The four-grade comparison keeps the posterior-mean order and changes the allowed family. Its risk is comparable under the same law, τ and weight, but its order-based optimum is not a global optimum over every four-grade report. The two compared families are not nested. Withholding can reflect several interacting restrictions; the page does not assign a single exclusive cause to every shared-grade pair.
Data: California Department of Education, 2026 California School Dashboard chronic absenteeism data, academic year 2025–26, as adapted in postrank 1.1.0 (pr_case_cde). This deliberately spread twelve-school teaching subset is conditional on a statewide prior fitted to 5,834 eligible schools; prior-estimation uncertainty is not propagated. CDE source conditions apply; the data are not relicensed, are provided as is without warranty, and imply no CDE endorsement.
The analysis concerns directional reporting of chronic absence within this subset. It neither computes Dashboard status-and-change colours nor establishes school quality, causal effects, statewide optimality or calibration. Shared grades do not imply equal absence probabilities.

title: School tertiles and minimum-risk grades
text: Two boundaries partition the posterior-mean order of twelve schools into a grade report. The display evaluates this fixed report and compares it with the minimum-risk report over all assignments using at most three grades at the same τ. Grade 1 states lower chronic absence under the supplied posterior. Boundary changes alter both the number and identity of the stated directions. The comparison therefore separates a conventional grouping along one order from optimisation over the full capped family, while preserving the same posterior and reporting loss.

title: School tertiles and minimum-risk grades
text:
Numerical illustrations

Tertiles splits the schools into three groups of four. It states 48 pairs, expects 1.829 wrong directions and has risk .082255; the browser optimum states 45 pairs with risk .063774.
Archived grades puts the cuts after positions 3 and 9. These reproduce the archived three-grade report: 45 stated pairs and risk .063774. The relation-change table has no changed pairs.
One boundary puts both controls at position 6. One distinct boundary gives two grades, 36 stated pairs and risk .091293.
Higher withholding cost raises τ to .45. The optimum now states 47 pairs and has risk .143197. The changed-pair table identifies the resulting relation changes.

The cut positions describe a fixed report along one order. The comparison enumerates every report with at most three grades, including other orders. Its average-error bound belongs to that exact optimum at the displayed τ; it is not a per-pair certainty threshold for the tertiles. Reports can disclose different amounts while being evaluated under the same loss.
The dots and intervals summarize the supplied school posterior. A shared grade withholds directions and does not assert equal chronic-absence probabilities. Rows inside a grade remain in posterior-mean order for reading, with no additional reported comparisons.
Data: California Department of Education, 2026 California School Dashboard chronic absenteeism data, academic year 2025–26, as adapted in postrank 1.1.0 (pr_case_cde). This deliberately spread twelve-school teaching subset is conditional on a statewide prior fitted to 5,834 eligible schools; prior-estimation uncertainty is not propagated. CDE source conditions apply; the data are not relicensed, are provided as is without warranty, and imply no CDE endorsement.
The analysis concerns directional reporting of chronic absence within this subset. It neither computes Dashboard status-and-change colours nor establishes school quality, causal effects, statewide optimality or calibration. Shared grades do not imply equal absence probabilities.

title: postrank Explorer
text:
Ranking uncertain quantities requires decisions about which comparisons to report. A strict ranking states a direction for every pair of units. An ordered grade report states directions between grades and withholds comparisons within grades. The resulting report can be evaluated by its posterior expected errors and its extent of disclosure.
This website examines these decisions using postrank, an R package for posterior ranking with integer grades. The applications cover posterior inputs, reporting losses, coherence constraints, alternative reporting rules and multiple criteria. Numerical illustrations use specified posterior distributions and released empirical examples. Each calculation is conditional on the posterior and report family stated with its result.

title: postrank Explorer
text:
Organisation


Ranking under uncertainty. Sampling variation, posterior shrinkage, pairwise probabilities and alternative ranking summaries. The normal–normal example examines how precision affects posterior ordering.
From ranks to grades. Pairwise decisions, coherent grade reports, reporting risk and the error–disclosure frontier. Withholding cost specifies the relative cost of leaving a comparison unstated.
Common rules. Evaluation of tiers, evidence flags and posterior cuts under a common reporting loss. Matched-disclosure comparisons distinguish additional expected errors from differences in the number of statements.
Several criteria. Common reports selected using criterion weights, error budgets or minimax risk. The two-score example gives the corresponding criterion-specific error profiles.
Cases. Firm contact gaps, school chronic absence and historical county outcomes. The school example compares tertiles with minimum-risk grades under a fixed posterior.
Tools. Calculation from supplied posterior summaries and specification of reports for released cases. The case-report tool retains targets, settings, computation scope and source information in its exports.


The catalogue indexes applications by part, concept and data source. Application numbers give the part and position within it; for example, 1.3 denotes the third application in Part 1. Each application has named presets, a numerical-illustration section and a standalone version. Downloaded standalone versions also operate without a network connection.

title: postrank Explorer
text:
Numerical verification
Browser calculations are compared with postrank 1.1.0 results and independent base-R calculations that use neither postrank nor the JavaScript engine. Released data have recorded sources, fields, licences and checksums. Page checks reproduce the specified numerical illustrations and compare their quoted values with the displayed results. Inputs and comparison code are retained in verification/ and r-export/ in the source repository.
Result labels identify the family searched when a report is selected. Numerical agreement is assessed for the defined examples and tolerances; it does not establish correctness for every input or calibration of a supplied posterior model. Source notes give the conditioning assumptions and scope of the empirical illustrations.

title: A common report for Alabama county outcomes
text: A common report evaluates Alabama counties on historical income and incarceration outcomes. The weight sets the relative cost of criterion errors. The map and table connect grades with marginal intervals. Grade 1 denotes higher income and lower incarceration. The live search uses weighted expected-rank cuts; archived reports and commonality-cost bounds retain their original optimisation scope.

title: A common report for Alabama county outcomes
text:
Numerical illustrations

“Equal weights.” Crenshaw County is alone in grade one; Montgomery and Russell share grade five; the shares expected wrong are .0520 on income and .172 on incarceration. Grade one means favourable historical outcomes: higher income and lower incarceration, rather than greater need.
“Income only.” The report states 1,769 of 2,211 pairs, while its share expected wrong on incarceration rises to .349. “Income .80” brings that share to .305 and income’s to .0305; risks at different weights belong to different losses.
“Fixed income D1.” Its grades stay fixed at equal weights, with risk .1906; D2’s risk is .1998. The corresponding archived map can be displayed beside the selected common-report map.
“Color counties by this report.” The display accepts an archived baseline or an edited grade vector. The complete table shows every county’s grades and marginal intervals; the relation summary compares it with archived P. “Incarceration only” gives shares .312 on income and .0873 on incarceration.

The live search is best along the current weighted expected-rank order, which combines the criteria’s posterior average positions. At the original cost and cap, it reproduces archived P at equal weights, D1 for income alone and D2 for incarceration alone. The app retains their solver status and bounds. The archived commonality table answers a separate question: the increase in each criterion’s risk under the original common report relative to its separate optimum. Its bounds belong to that original loss and full capped family, when a different live setting is selected.






Outcomes condition on parents’ income at percentile 25, with race and gender pooled, for cohorts born 1978–83: household income in 2014–15 and incarceration on 1 April 2010. These are historical associations, rather than current conditions, causal effects of places, need or eligibility. Separate criterion fits do not supply a joint posterior. Data: Chetty, Friedman, Hendren, Jones and Porter (2022), Opportunity Atlas replication, Harvard Dataverse doi:10.7910/DVN/NKCQM1; Opportunity Insights and U.S. Census Bureau, CC BY 4.0; as adapted in postrank 1.1.0. Changes: Alabama filtering, favorable target orientation, supplied marginal summaries, archived reports and browser searches. Boundaries: U.S. Census Bureau Cartographic Boundary Files 2025, public domain, via usmapdata 1.1.0. No endorsement implied.

title: School reports at matched disclosure
text: Matched disclosure gives a different comparison from risk at a common withholding cost. Three grades for twelve schools state at most 48 pairs. The display gives the expected-error range at each disclosure and the complete distribution of reports stating 48 pairs, including the tertiles. A lower convex boundary permits mixtures of complete reports. The maximum-disclosure constraint explains why randomisation cannot improve on the least-error member at that endpoint.

title: School reports at matched disclosure
text:
Numerical illustrations

At the tertiles’ disclosure shows all 34,650 reports at N = 48. The tertiles have the smallest E, 1.829; the next report has E = 1.909.
Between feasible disclosures selects N = 46. No single report in this family states exactly 46 pairs, while the lower hull reaches H = .4551 by a mixture with weight .500 on the more-disclosing report.
A lower mixture selects N = 30. The hull value is .005174, using weight .167 on the more-disclosing endpoint.
Other cuts, full range places cuts at 1 and 2. The selected report states 21 pairs and expects 1.116 wrong directions; the enlarged axis shows the complete ranges at every disclosure.

For twelve units, at most three grades allow at most 48 stated pairs. Reaching that maximum requires three groups of four. Any mixture with expected disclosure 48 must therefore use reports at that maximum; averaging them cannot improve on their least-error member. This explains why randomisation cannot improve on the tertiles at their own disclosure.
The hull mixes complete reports before one is selected. Such a mixture is not itself a single deterministic grade report. Its weight belongs to that reporting mixture, with the larger-disclosure endpoint explicitly named. The histogram and keyboard table show the complete error distribution, while the five-report table identifies its least-error tail.
Data: California Department of Education, 2026 California School Dashboard chronic absenteeism data, academic year 2025–26, as adapted in postrank 1.1.0 (pr_case_cde). This deliberately spread twelve-school teaching subset is conditional on a statewide prior fitted to 5,834 eligible schools; prior-estimation uncertainty is not propagated. CDE source conditions apply; the data are not relicensed, are provided as is without warranty, and imply no CDE endorsement.
The analysis concerns directional reporting of chronic absence within this subset. It neither computes Dashboard status-and-change colours nor establishes school quality, causal effects, statewide optimality or calibration. Shared grades do not imply equal absence probabilities.

title: School-report changes along the withholding-cost path
text: With the posterior and report family fixed, minimum-risk school reports change at specific withholding costs. The path records total disclosure and every newly stated, newly withheld or reversed comparison at each change. Exact optimal disclosure is nondecreasing in τ under these conditions, but individual relations need not be retained. The display distinguishes the exact browser path from archived solver results, preserving the status and gap of each archived solve. Boundary tables include equal-risk reports and transitions below the slider’s displayed minimum.

title: School-report changes along the withholding-cost path
text:
Numerical illustrations

The usual setting uses τ .20. The optimum states 45 pairs in groups of sizes 3, 6, 3.
Past the last interior boundary uses τ .45. The optimum states 47 pairs in groups of sizes 4, 5, 3; the complete pair-change list gives the altered relations.
The early boundaries keeps the slider at its low end. The exact boundaries near .000162 and .000263 lie below that minimum but remain in the tables, including the step to 27 pairs.
The upper endpoint reaches τ .50. The path still states 47 pairs, and the chart retains all 13 archived solves.

The posterior, criterion weight and at-most-three-grade family stay fixed along this path. Exact optimal disclosure is nondecreasing in τ under those conditions. Individual relationships can change in more than one way, which is why the tables retain newly withheld and reversed pairs as well as new statements.
Changing τ changes the loss. A risk printed at one step is evaluated at that step’s own τ; cross-setting risk differences therefore concern different losses. At a boundary the app also lists all returned equal-risk reports and the comparison tolerance. The archived dots use the same family but were obtained with HiGHS, so their solver-status and gap fields remain separate from exact enumeration.

title: Equivalent reporting-loss scales
text: The complete six-site family contains 4,683 coherent reports. Each is evaluated under KRW’s loss at reward λ and postrank’s risk at the corresponding withholding cost τ. The scatter compares these two evaluations and identifies their minimising sets. Under the stated tie-free and common-family conditions, an increasing affine transformation relates the objectives, so their optimal reports coincide. The grid check repeats this comparison across cost settings. An additional archived firm card is evaluated as a fixed report and retains the distinction between its original selection probabilities and the released evaluation probabilities.

title: Equivalent reporting-loss scales
text:
Numerical illustrations

λ 1, flat line gives slope 0. The full order 1/2/3/4/5/6 has DR .0480 and expected correct minus wrong per pair .904. KRW call these minimising grades Condorcet ranks. The separate 97-firm grid card is evaluated as a fixed report.
λ .25 gives slope 3. Both objectives choose 1/2/3/3/4/5, with postrank risk .0372. The ring marks a coherent report, rather than a collection of independent pair decisions.
τ .25, whole grid checks every report at every one of 49 τ settings. The two complete minimising sets agree at 49 of 49 values. The table gives the corresponding decimal λ and complete grade vectors for both objectives.
λ .08 gives τ .0741 and 1/1/2/2/3/3. More pairs share a grade when a correct direction earns less.
τ .40 moves the other slider: λ becomes 2/3 and the full order returns. Arrow keys on the figure read every report, including reports away from the best line.

The correspondence requires a tie-free target and the same posterior probabilities, orientation, units and report family. For every such report, postrank’s risk at τ equals τ plus one minus τ times KRW’s risk at the matching λ. The reported residual checks this identity over the complete family; it measures floating-point rounding, not posterior calibration. Equal-risk tolerances determine which reports remain in each minimising set.
The additional KRW card uses released probabilities for evaluation, while KRW’s code chose it under archived probabilities. It is not claimed to be optimal here. Changes: postrank 1.1.0 midpoint-cell pair probabilities; archived λ-grid cards retained. No endorsement is implied. These data describe the historical correspondence experiment, not any firm’s current conduct.

title: Firm-pair probabilities and report-card blocks
text: Each cell contains the posterior probability that the row firm’s contact gap exceeds the column firm’s gap. The matrix includes every ordered pair and the diagonal. Thresholding identifies directions that would minimise loss for each pair considered separately. The archived card’s grade blocks identify the statements in a coherent report. Comparing the two reveals high-probability directions withheld within grades and additional directions stated between grades. The probability scale is retained throughout; darker blue represents greater support for the row-above-column direction rather than a larger error probability.

title: Firm-pair probabilities and report-card blocks
text:
Numerical illustrations

All direction probabilities. The Blues legend is labelled “Pr(row truly higher)”. A darker cell means a larger direction probability; it does not mean a larger error. Arrow keys move through the complete matrix, and each cell names both firms and the card’s relation.
Above the threshold. At λ .25, the corresponding withholding cost is τ .20. The strict pairwise rule would state 1,575 pairs whose favored direction has probability above .80. Other cells fade, while the grey diagonal continues to mark self-comparisons.
Add the card blocks. The card withholds 575 bright pairs inside its blocks. It also states 324 pairs whose error exceeds τ. These are consequences of fitting directions into one coherent report, not a cap on grades.
λ .50 blocks. The threshold admits 2,994 pairs. Of these, 49 are withheld by the card; 545 stated pairs have error above the current τ. Varying the reward changes both the threshold and the selected archived card.
Gender blocks. The target is the signed male-name contact advantage. Negative gaps favor female-named applicants. Both row-above-column directions retain this signed orientation.







Grid cards were computed with KRW’s code under archived probabilities and solver tolerances. Their evaluations here use the released postrank probabilities and supply no new optimality certificate. Race’s baseline card is Figure 7; gender is Figure 14 (§VIII). Figures 5A and 6 are in §V.E, and Figure 10A is in §VI.B.

title: A common report for race and gender gaps
text: A common report can state directions for the same firms on both race and gender contact gaps. The race weight sets the relative contribution of the two criteria’s wrong-direction counts. The scatter displays the selected grades, and the risk chart compares the common report with KRW’s two fixed cards under the current loss. The live search uses contiguous cuts of the weighted expected-rank order. At the original settings, its result agrees with the archived common solve; this agreement does not establish unrestricted optimality at other settings.

title: A common report for race and gender gaps
text:
Numerical illustrations

“Equal weights.” At the original cost, the common report’s risk .2455 is below the all-withheld risk; neither published card does.
“Race .80.” The race card crosses the withholding line near race weight .69. “Gender .80” shows the opposite crossing near .29.
“Color firms by this report.” The selected archived card is evaluated at the current cost. Its grades stay fixed while its evaluation changes. Firm selection in the scatter, selector or table gives both supplied marginal intervals.
“Most grades allowed in the live order search.” The family size and complete returned equal-risk sets are reported for each cap. Grade one is stated highest; sharing a grade withholds a comparison.

The live report minimises loss along the weighted expected-rank order: posterior average positions combined using the current weights. The order changes with those weights. At the original equal weights, cost and cap, it reproduces the archived common solve over all capped reports. Its status, bound and gap remain visible. Each published KRW card retains its own original selection setting; a larger current risk is a comparison under a different loss, without reassessing KRW’s selection under its original objective. See the original report card for that card’s interpretation.






The separate criterion fits supply marginal intervals and criterionwise expected loss; they do not supply a joint posterior across gaps. Across-firm correlation is not such a posterior. These experimental data do not describe firms’ current conduct. title: Signed and absolute gender-gap targets
text: A signed male-name contact advantage and its absolute magnitude are distinct reporting targets. A large female-name advantage is low on the signed scale but large on the absolute scale. Each target has its own released posterior pair probabilities, expected-rank order and optimal cuts within that order. The display compares the resulting relations and marginal summaries for all firms. Folding a posterior distribution also differs from taking the absolute value of its mean. Consequently, the absolute-target report cannot be recovered from the signed means or direction probabilities alone.

title: Signed and absolute gender-gap targets
text:
Numerical illustrations

Both target-specific cards. Both computations use at most 4 grades at withholding cost τ .20. The family label beside each result specifies that each is labelled “optimal within this order.” The two orders can differ, so neither result is a certificate of optimality over every possible report.
Every changed pair. The “Complete list of changed unordered pairs” keeps every relation that changes from the signed report to the absolute report. A direction can appear, disappear or reverse. Each row names both firms and shows the wrong-direction probability under the law for that report. These are different targets, so their risk values are not a comparison under one fixed loss.
All firm summaries. “All firms in released ID order” keeps all 97 firms together. The table keeps the supplied means and central 90% intervals for both targets, their expected ranks and their chosen grades. A folded posterior mean is not obtained by taking the absolute value of a signed posterior mean.

The report cards use supplied marginal intervals only to describe individual firms. Their grades come from pair probabilities, the declared order, the cap and the withholding cost. Sharing a grade states no direction; it does not assert equality. The folded probabilities come directly from the public postrank data object’s absolute-gender alternative. The app does not refit independent normal distributions to those summaries or infer a joint race–gender posterior from marginal information.
Both precision views keep the signed gender estimate’s original sampling SE. Beside the folded report, it is only a precision covariate, not an SE of the absolute target. A shared middle grade is not evidence of average behavior.






The two reports are newly computed cuts of their own expected-rank orders. They are not KRW’s archived cards. title: Criterion-specific excess risk of a common report
text: Requiring a common report can raise each criterion’s risk relative to the report it would select separately. The commonality cost is this difference, evaluated within the same family and at the same withholding cost. The connectors compare each criterion’s separate minimum with its risk under the common report. Equal error weights need not imply equal commonality costs. The live examples calculate the relevant reports directly; the larger archived examples retain the recorded optimisation bounds. These costs concern reporting risk and do not have an intrinsic welfare interpretation.

title: Criterion-specific excess risk of a common report
text:
Numerical illustrations

Equal weights. The excess risks are .0490 on score A and .0145 on score B. Each connector joins the criterion-specific optimum to its common-report evaluation. The comparison table keeps each criterion’s risk separate from its wrong share.
Score A only. The common report is score A’s own best, so score A has zero excess risk and score B has excess risk .1481. Score B still has its own comparison; a zero error weight does not remove that criterion from the display.
w .70. The common report becomes {A} > {B, C, D} > {E, F}: the excess risks are .0253 on score A and .0563 on score B. Moving a weight changes the objective used to select the common report.
Score B only. Two common reports tie. Score A has excess risk .1580 under one and .1697 under the other; score B has zero excess risk. Both common reports and both of score B’s own optima are shown, with their equal-risk tolerance.
Thirty sites, higher price. The archived common report states 276 pairs. Snap’s cost is .4455, and its expected wrong share among those stated directions is .784. The cost interval comes from optimisation bounds.
Thirty sites, lower price. The common report withholds every direction, yet each criterion could prefer a report of its own. Costs are .0895, .0749 and .1022 for poverty, frl and snap, respectively.







The cost is a postrank package quantity, Δₖ: it carries no welfare meaning, and a large cost does not by itself say that a weight is wrong. The thirty-site results are fixed draw-based archives with their recorded settings, statuses and bounds. They are separate from the Gaussian marginal example. Their intervals describe optimisation accuracy, not posterior uncertainty; missing own-report grade vectors are not reconstructed.

library(postrank)
cc <- postrank_commonality_cost(postrank(pr_tutorial$two, weights=c(score_A=.5,score_B=.5), tau=.2, G_max=3, backend="highs", report_card=FALSE, fragility=FALSE), backend="highs")
cc$table[, c("criterion_id", "cost_lower", "cost_upper")]
