title: Opposing criterion directions
text: Criteria can support opposite directions for a given pair. The matrix identifies these disagreements by comparing forward and reverse error probabilities on each criterion. The bars evaluate the weighted costs of both strict directions and withholding. Supplied normal posteriors and finite known-state examples distinguish disagreement within a state from uncertainty about that state. The smaller posterior expected directional cost can reflect both sources, and is therefore not generally a measure of criterion conflict alone. A complete coherent report imposes constraints beyond this isolated-pair comparison.

title: Opposing criterion directions
text:
Numerical illustrations

Six sites, B–C. The equal-weight costs are .4841 for B above C and .5159 for C above B. The map has 3 opposing pairs. Withholding is cheaper for this pair on its own, but these actions do not yet form a common grade.
Thirty sites. There are 397 opposing pairs. For the selected pair, the smaller expected directional cost is .3652. Each criterion has equal error weight; the table keeps its separate errors visible.
Certain opposition. The two directions each cost .5000; withholding costs .2000. Here the smaller directional cost is also the statewise conflict quantity. The additional boundary preset shows every action sharing the minimum when withholding has the same cost.
Uncertain agreement. The smaller posterior directional cost is still .5000, but statewise γ is .0000 in each state. The criteria agree within every state; uncertainty about which state holds creates the directional cost.
Zero error weight. The opposing pair stays on the map, while its cheaper direction costs .0000 and the reverse costs 1.0000. A disagreement on a criterion with zero weight does not itself force weighted error.
Latent equality. One criterion’s reverse errors are .600 and .900, both above one half, yet it prefers the smaller one. The other criterion prefers the opposite direction. Both weighted directions cost .7500; comparing errors with their reverse detects this disagreement even with equality mass.







A strict direction counts as wrong at equality. The map compares forward and reverse errors on every criterion; it does not use a one-half threshold or discard criteria with zero weight. Statewise γ excludes withholding. Posterior uncertainty and substantive conflict need not have a unique additive decomposition. A full coherent report can choose differently from an isolated pair.









TipIn postrank





library(postrank)
pr_tutorial$two$e["B", "C", ]



Standalone: open this app, for example ?preset=uncertain&theme=dark.
Related applications: Posterior profiles on multiple criteria · The decision for an isolated pair.

title: Pairwise errors from joint posterior draws
text: A posterior draw contains one joint state of every unit on every criterion. The empirical error probability of a proposed direction is the proportion of states in which that direction is wrong. The package’s 32-state toy sample illustrates the role of alignment: cyclically shifting one unit’s vector preserves its marginal values but changes its pairing with the other units. Shifting all units together instead permutes complete states and preserves full-sample pairwise errors. The display records both counts and denominators, including the effects of using only a prefix of the retained sample.

title: Pairwise errors from joint posterior draws
text:
Numerical illustrations

Original states. Among the 32 retained states, placing 001 above site-B is wrong 8 times on need_A and 32 times on need_B. The empirical error shares are .250 and 1. Each complete state specifies the order of all three units on both criteria.
Shift one unit. Moving site-B’s whole two-criterion vector forward cyclically changes the need_A count to 7 times and its share to .219. The need_B count remains 32 times. The raw marginal values have only been reordered; the joint pairing has changed.
Move states together. Applying the same shift to every unit restores the original full-sample counts: 8 times and 32 times. This is a reordering of complete states, so every full-sample coefficient stays the same.
Short prefix. Only 8 retained states now enter the estimates. Both the wrong count and denominator depend on the selected prefix length. Short prefixes can change even when complete states are shifted together.
Unshifted pair. The pair 001 and site C contains neither shifted unit. Its counts remain 0 times and 25 times, with need_B share .781. Changing a third unit’s pairing cannot change this pair’s comparisons.
Full cycle. A full cyclic shift returns every source vector to its original row, with counts 8 times and 32 times again. The source table retains all original unit and criterion coordinates.







This is a fixed IID numerical sample from a specified synthetic normal law. A zero empirical error share means that the event did not occur in this sample; it does not establish an exact zero posterior probability. The shift is a reproducible dependence illustration, not an additional posterior simulation or a convergence test.









NoteIn postrank





library(postrank)
e <- postrank_pairwise(postrank_toy)$e
e["001", "site-B", ]  # need_A .25, need_B 1



Standalone: Pairwise errors from joint posterior draws.
Related applications: Marginal summaries and joint direction probabilities · Monte Carlo error in pairwise probabilities.

title: Error budgets under estimated pairwise probabilities
text: A report can satisfy an error budget on estimated pairwise probabilities and violate it under the stipulated exact law. The budget concerns the expected wrong share among stated pairs. Given a proposed uniform bound on probability error, tighter and looser estimated thresholds define inner and outer feasible families. The display checks the coefficient bound and the resulting inclusions separately, alongside an advisory numerical tolerance. A fixed-size independent-draw illustration distinguishes a probabilistic numerical error guarantee from the deterministic membership calculations. Neither calculation establishes calibration of the supplied posterior model.

title: Error budgets under estimated pairwise probabilities
text:
Numerical illustrations

Estimated pass. For A above B, the estimated wrong share is .200 and the exact supplied-law share is .300. The budget is .25. Its estimated row passes while its exact row fails; the inner threshold .15 and outer threshold .35 remain separate on the number line.
Negative inner. The signed inner threshold is −.05, even though the estimated wrong share is 0. Replacing this threshold with zero would wrongly admit A above B. The all-withheld report still passes the count-form tests, with no defined wrong share.
Exactly two. Requiring two grades removes all-withheld. The inner family has 0 reports; the exact family also happens to be empty here. Their separate counters matter: an empty inner family alone would not establish exact infeasibility.
Radius too small. The proposed radius is reduced to .05 with the exact law unchanged. The coefficient checks read “no,” and an inner member fails the exact budget. The app displays the actual inclusion counterexample rather than assuming the bracket.
Raw comparisons. With advisory tolerance removed, its coefficient check reads “no.” At the default radius, the tiny raw excess explains why the strict check fails while the tolerant comparison passes. The actual inclusions are separate tests, not consequences of accepting a soft tolerance.
Fixed-S IID. The separate illustration uses 1,000 whole-state draws from the six-site independent normal law, reusing the Monte Carlo producer and bound. Score B has error weight 0 but remains protected by its .03 budget. Requiring exactly two grades gives an empty inner family while the exact family remains nonempty.







“Exact” means the stipulated supplied law. The main two-unit example declares coefficients deterministically and makes no sampling-probability claim. In the IID illustration, the fixed-size simultaneous coefficient event has probability at least one minus α across repeated numerical samples from the same law. This concerns numerical approximation, not model calibration or a posterior probability of compliance. Signed thresholds are never clipped.



Standalone: Error budgets under estimated pairwise probabilities.
Related applications: Criterion-specific expected-error budgets · Monte Carlo error in pairwise probabilities.

title: Quantities not identified by pairwise probabilities
text: Pairwise probabilities determine the additive expected risk of a fixed report. They do not generally identify the probability that all statements are correct, or the direction of a composite based on target magnitudes. The finite examples vary the coupling between complete criterion states while preserving each criterion’s entire two-unit law. Consequently, additive risks remain fixed while composite and joint-event probabilities can change. Evaluation of a selected fixed report separates these effects from report optimisation. Additional joint-law information is required to interpret such events from marginal or pairwise releases.

title: Quantities not identified by pairwise probabilities
text:
Numerical illustrations

Together: each disclosed direction has additive risk .5000. For A above B, the probability that both criteria are right is .5. The displayed state masses belong to entire arrays; they do not describe independently drawn criterion columns.
Opposite: the additive risk stays .5000, while both the forward composite error and the probability of being right on every criterion become 0. The composite is always positive, although the criteria point opposite ways within each state. The full table retains all reporting actions.
Halfway: the all-criteria probability is .25. The wrong-count distribution changes with the coupling even though its expectation and every report’s additive risk stay fixed. Error weights and withholding cost remain separate controls; changing them changes the loss.
One zero error weight: the probability of zero weighted wrong count is .5, while all-criteria correctness is 0. A criterion given zero error weight still belongs to the all-criteria event. The two event labels therefore cannot be exchanged.
Select withholding: the wrong or correct fraction reads “NA: no disclosure.” The joint no-error events hold vacuously because the report makes no statements. This supplies no accuracy claim.
Five statements: the fixed report’s mean weighted fraction correct is .87, but the probability all its statements are right on every criterion is .75. It makes 5 statements. The second state has weighted wrong count 2.6; the criterion grid gives its whole-state probability and contribution to the average.







Note



These are stipulated finite teaching laws, with larger oriented target values meaning higher reporting priority. The joint-law editor preserves the claimed marginal laws by construction. Pair arrays alone do not identify a missing coupling, composite posterior or joint event; marginal-only empirical releases cannot supply those quantities. The best-report and full cross-loss views below provide separate optimisation context for the selected fixed report.


Open standalone, for example ?preset=opposite&theme=dark.
Related applications: Composite targets and criterion directions, Opposing criterion directions.

title: A common grade report for two scores
text: A common report evaluates wrong directions with weight w on score A and 1 − w on score B. Withholding costs τ once per pair. The lines between posterior means identify units whose orders differ across scores. For each weight, withholding cost and grade cap, the display gives the selected common report, its pairwise relation and its two criterion-specific error profiles. Thus, a common grade assignment can be evaluated separately on each score even though a weighted objective selects it. Shared grades withhold comparisons under both criteria.

title: A common grade report for two scores
text:
Numerical illustrations

Equal weights. The report states 9 pairs at risk .0933. Its expected wrong shares are .0177 on score A and .0267 on score B. The outlined pair errors show why low-cost isolated directions need not appear in a coherent report.
No cap. Searching all 4,683 reports still gives the same 9 stated pairs. At these settings, transitivity of shared grades explains the withheld comparisons; the cap does not.
A-heavy. Giving score A more weight restores the three blocks {A, B} > {C, D} > {E, F}, stating 12 pairs. The profile shows the consequence for each score separately.
Score A only. The report follows score A’s order between its blocks. On score B an expected .237 of its stated directions are wrong, although score B contributes no error cost.
w .70. The common report keeps {B, C, D} together; score B’s expected wrong share is .115. Its pairwise relations differ from those at equal weights.
Score B only. The best report is tied with another report. The expected wrong share on score A is .200 under the first and .215 under the other; both reports and full profiles appear.







Note



These are illustrative independent normal posteriors. Grade one means highest priority; a shared grade withholds a direction rather than asserting equality. The mean bound concerns an expected average over stated pairs, not every pair. Changing weights changes the loss, so risks at different weights correspond to different objectives.








TipIn postrank





library(postrank)
two <- postrank(pr_tutorial$two, weights = c(score_A=.5, score_B=.5), tau=.2, G_max=3L, backend="highs")
get_grades(two); get_profile(two)[c("criterion", "E_over_N", "risk")]



Standalone: two-scores, for example ?w=.5&tau=.2&cap=all.
Related applications: Reporting risk and withholding cost.

title: Reasons for a withheld comparison
text: A shared grade withholds a direction without asserting equality or proximity of the true values. The pair display compares its isolated-pair actions with complete coherent reports under the specified family. Four diagnostics consider posterior uncertainty, opposing criteria, effects on other reported pairs and family restrictions. These conditions are not mutually exclusive. Requiring a direction and reoptimising the full report gives its additional risk, rather than a unique causal attribution for withholding. The empirical views retain the target definitions and conditioning assumptions of their released posterior inputs.

title: Reasons for a withheld comparison
text:
Numerical illustrations

Coherence: the six-site report withholds A–B even though its isolated forward cost is below the withholding cost. The minimum-cost complete report stating A above B has risk .1019, an increase of .008513. Removing the cap does not remove this difference. The signed changed-pair account records the other altered statements.
Certain conflict: each criterion is certain about B–C, but they point opposite ways. Requiring B above C produces risk .1667, an increase of .025. The reverse direction is a separate search with a different full report and cost.
Uncertainty: the two criteria agree within every stipulated state. Their directional expected costs are .4000 and .6000, while each known state’s smaller directional cost is zero. Uncertainty across states differs from disagreement within a state.
Fixed order: B above C is feasible along the declared order, but its minimum-cost report has risk .3167. The unrestricted family provides a separate comparison. Under Indivisible block, requiring those two units to stay together makes both directions infeasible.
CDE subset: all 523,251 reports with at most three grades belong to the declared search. Forward and reverse requirements are evaluated separately. This deliberately spread teaching subset and its fixed statewide prior do not establish a statewide optimum or a school-quality judgement.
KRW fixed order: the search contains 147,537 contiguous-cut reports. The cap relaxation keeps the very same expected-rank order; it does not search unrestricted reports. These newly produced postrank reports differ from KRW’s archived cards.







Note



Every probability and risk conditions on the supplied law. Case views display their full released attribution, conditioning and licence notices: CDE source conditions apply; KRW is noncommercial use only under CC-BY-NC, with no endorsement implied. A positive extra risk is a comparison within a declared family, not a unique causal explanation for withholding.


Open standalone, for example ?preset=fixed-order.
Related applications: Opposing criterion directions, A common grade report for two scores, Posterior summaries in a grade report.

title: Evaluation under an alternative posterior law
text: The posterior used to choose a report may differ from the law used to evaluate it. Here the selection law remains fixed while the evaluation mean of one site, or all evaluation standard deviations, are varied. The selected report is held fixed and scored under both laws. Its evaluation risk is also compared with the minimum under the evaluation law over the same report family. This separates a change in the risk of a given report from regret relative to an alternative report. Neither specified law is assumed to describe an external population exactly.

title: Evaluation under an alternative posterior law
text:
Numerical illustrations

Same laws. The selected report has risk .0417 under either law, and evaluation regret is 0. The plotted intervals and means coincide; the largest pair-error gap is also 0. This is the point from which each disagreement can be read.
Move C upward. The frozen report’s evaluation risk rises to .1360, while the evaluation-best report has risk .0542. Their difference, .0817, is the regret. The chosen reports change 3 pair decisions. The table separates the two evaluations of each report.
Wider evaluation law. The frozen report now has risk .0779, yet regret remains 0. It is still best in the family under the evaluation law. A change in the risk of a report does not by itself imply that another report should replace it.
C +.40, no cap. Evaluation regret is .0108. Both optimisations now search the larger family; the family tags identify their common comparison domain. The bound keeps this family fixed while changing the law.
Small change, new report. A pair-error radius of .0132 accompanies 1 changed pair decision. Regret is only .0008, beneath the uniform bound .0263. A small objective gap can coexist with different grade vectors.







The laws here are independent normals specified for teaching. Neither is asserted to be the true law of an external population. The general bound is twice a justified uniform risk-discrepancy bound plus a valid optimiser gap over the whole common family. That gap concerns selection-law optimisation and is zero here; evaluation regret concerns the other law. Exact enumeration supplies the selection-law minimum; more posterior draws cannot establish agreement between the laws.









TipIn postrank





library(postrank)
g <- c(A=1L,B=1L,C=2L,D=2L,E=3L,F=3L)
postrank_evaluate(g, pr_tutorial$one, weights=c(score_A=1), tau=.2)$weighted_risk # .04165164



Standalone: two evaluation laws, for example ?shift=1&unit=C.
Related applications: Reporting risk and withholding cost, Monte Carlo error in pairwise probabilities.

title: Selection and evaluation using posterior draws
text: Each repetition draws from a specified posterior distribution, selects a grade report using estimated pairwise probabilities, and evaluates that fixed report twice. The first evaluation uses the selection draws; the second uses the exact law. Their signed difference can be positive or negative in an individual repetition. The selected point identifies the report held fixed in this comparison. Separate discrepancy and regret bounds distinguish error in its risk estimate from excess risk relative to the exact-law optimum in the same family.

title: Selection and evaluation using posterior draws
text:
Numerical illustrations

Own draws. Among these reruns, 33 look worse on their own draws. The followed run instead has gap −.00061: its selection draws make its chosen report look slightly better than the exact law does.
Looks worse. Another selected report from the same experiment has a positive discrepancy. Its gap is +.00072, even though it minimises risk for its own estimated probabilities. A single run need not look optimistic.
More draws. With 4,000 draws per run, the followed gap is −.00025. The cloud and coefficient radius describe the remaining numerical variation. Realized errors need not shrink on every step.
Tighter family. Search the 603 reports with at most three grades. The followed gap is +.00102. Both evaluations still refer to that run’s same selected report. The grey intervals show how loose the discrepancy bounds can be.
Both scores. The two scores receive equal weights. The followed gap is −.00322. The discrepancy radius now averages each score’s largest pair-error discrepancy with those same weights.

The grey intervals bound the absolute gap of each selected report. The regret readout asks a different question: how much worse its exact-law risk is than the exact-law minimum in the same family. Its bound includes an allowance for numerical optimisation. A small risk difference does not require identical grades.






These are independent draws from fictional normal posteriors, not repeated observed datasets. “Exact” refers to the declared law. The separate package toy table evaluates each fold’s selected report on the other fold; it neither corrects the full-data risk nor checks the fitted model against new observations.









TipIn postrank





library(postrank)
cf <- postrank_crossfit(postrank_toy, settings=postrank_settings(weights=c(need_A=.6,need_B=.4),tau=.25,G_max=3L), backend="highs")
cf[c("mean_optimism", "mean_abs_optimism")]
This reproduces the separate package fold example, not the browser’s six-site draws.



Standalone: open the app, for example ?S=100&seed=1&run=6.
Related applications: Monte Carlo error in pairwise probabilities · Evaluation under an alternative posterior law.

title: Coherence constraints on pairwise decisions
text: Decisions that minimise loss separately for each pair need not correspond to a coherent grade report. Three independent normal posteriors for A, B and C provide an example. Varying B’s mean changes the pairwise direction probabilities and their loss-minimising actions at withholding cost τ. The density panel describes the posterior specification. The remaining panels compare the unconstrained pairwise minimum with the minimum over ordered grade reports. Their difference is the additional expected cost imposed by coherence, which requires all pair decisions to be represented by a single ordered partition.

title: Coherence constraints on pairwise decisions
text:
Numerical illustrations

Middle at 1.00. A–B and B–C are withheld separately, while A above C has probability .921 and is stated. Transitivity of shared grades contradicts that direction. The minimum coherent risk is .1728. Both optimal reports beneath the curves resolve the conflict by stating an additional direction.
Middle at .50. B moves closer to C. The choices now form {A} > {B, C}, with risk .1410. The coherent report reaches the pairwise cost: no extra cost is needed to make the local decisions coherent.
Middle at .80. The mean is just outside the shaded band and the report reaches risk .1589. Additional displayed digits resolve probabilities near the decision boundary.
Middle at 1.00, τ .10. The withholding cost decreases. The best report is {A, B, C}, risk .1000; it withholds the confident outer pair too. The pairwise choices remain incompatible with a grade report, but the minimum-risk coherent resolution has changed.
Middle at 1.00, τ .25. The threshold falls to .75, below .760. Every pair is stated, the shaded band vanishes, and {A} > {B} > {C} represents the pairwise choices. The density panel is unchanged because τ affects the loss rather than the posterior.







Shared grades assert no equality of true values. They withhold directions, and sharing a grade is transitive. Kline, Rose and Walters call this a form of a “Condorcet cycle in indifferences”: the conflict is in the shared grades. These are posteriors set by hand for teaching. The browser evaluates every report of the stated family, lists equal-risk optima and gives their tolerance; the band is an aid to reading the picture, while compatibility is checked directly against the reports.



Standalone: coherence, for example ?omega2=.81&tau=.20.
Related applications: The decision for an isolated pair, Coherence in a finite three-unit example.

title: Expected and realised errors among stated directions
text: For a fixed report with N stated directions and expected wrong count E, the expected error share is E/N when N > 0. Posterior draws illustrate the variation of realised wrong counts around E. The probability that every statement is correct depends on the joint posterior distribution, whereas the expected count is a sum of pairwise error probabilities. The display also identifies the conditions under which optimality within a report family implies E ≤ τN. Withholding every pair gives an undefined error share because N is zero.

title: Expected and realised errors among stated directions
text:
Numerical illustrations

Start without draws. The report states 14 of 15 pairs, and its expected share wrong is .0255. The blue cells give the stated-pair errors. The optimality badge is reassessed after changes to the grades or eligible family.
Best report, draws. Across 100 draws, the mean count is .360 wrong directions per draw, with mean share .0257; the expected count is .3576. The matrix crosses the directions wrong in the final draw. The histogram counts draws, while the line shows their running average.
All withheld. The share reads “NA: no disclosure.” The all-right event is vacuous with probability 1; no direction is stated, so there is no error-share denominator. The drawn values remain visible, and the histogram records no wrong statements. The best-report button evaluates an alternative report on the same draws.
Three-unit law. The expected share wrong is 7/40, while B above C has error 1/4, above τ. The exact all-right probability is 3/4, with union lower bound 13/20. The final draw’s wrong share is 1/2.
Another coupling. The expected share stays 7/40, but the exact all-right probability becomes 13/20, meeting the same union lower bound. As the coupling varies, the order table, draws and zero histogram bin change together.

Changing the report keeps the same draws and scores them again. Changing τ changes the withholding charge without changing the report’s expected wrong count.






The badge appears only for an exact optimum of the shown family when that family includes the all-withheld report. Every report also shows the defined risk/count diagnostic, including when nothing is stated: E ≤ τN exactly when risk is at most τ. The six-site draws use independent normal latent values: their all-right values are Monte Carlo estimates, while the finite-law values and union bounds are exact. Both posteriors are stipulated; the joint-event interpretation and finite example follow the theory book, chapters 6 and 10.









TipIn postrank





library(postrank)
ev <- postrank_evaluate(c(A=1,B=2,C=3,D=3,E=4,F=5), pr_tutorial$one, weights=c(score_A=1), tau=.2)
ev[c("N", "E", "E_over_N")]



Standalone: open the app, for example ?draws=100&seed=1.
Related applications: Reporting risk and withholding cost · Grade reports as pairwise decisions.

title: Mixtures of frontier reports
text: Randomisation between two complete reports can attain intermediate points on the error–disclosure frontier. At a specified mean number of stated pairs, the diamond gives the mixture’s expected wrong count. The square gives the smallest error count among single reports at that disclosure, when such a report exists. The randomisation applies to the entire grade report, preserving coherence in each realisation. Its mean disclosure and mean error describe the distribution over reports rather than a further deterministic grade vector. The examples compare unrestricted and restricted report families.

title: Mixtures of frontier reports
text:
Numerical illustrations

Six sites, mean 10. The mixture selects the report stating 12 pairs with probability .50 and the report stating 8 pairs otherwise. The average error count is .01714. No single report states exactly this mean number of pairs: the diamond describes an average over reports rather than a new grade vector.
Six sites, mean 9. The more-disclosing report now has chance .25. The mixture expects .01332 wrong directions; the best single report at this disclosure expects .1597, a gap of .1464. The square and diamond share the same horizontal coordinate.
Six sites, mean 12. The selected point is a corner with .02477 expected wrong directions: no mixture is needed. Moving the mean-disclosure slider changes the lottery, while moving the withholding cost changes the supporting line and its best report.
Four units, mean 4. With two criteria, the quantities are expected weighted wrong directions. The mixture has 19/40 against the best single report’s 7/10, a gap of 9/40. Its two complete reports each have chance 1/2.
At most 3 grades, mean 9. The family has 603 reports and ends at 12 stated pairs. The unrestricted endpoint conclusion is not guaranteed for this family. The fixed-order example below gives a different reason that a restricted family can miss the unrestricted endpoint.







The half-cost endpoint requires the full report family and no latent ties on positive-weight criteria. The small fixed-order figure uses its own restricted boundary; it is not the unrestricted boundary. The six sites and finite laws are supplied examples, rather than fitted empirical posteriors.









TipIn postrank





library(postrank)
g <- list(c(A=1,B=1,C=2,D=2,E=2,F=2), c(A=1,B=1,C=2,D=2,E=3,F=3))
vapply(g, function(x) postrank_evaluate(x, pr_tutorial$one, weights=c(score_A=1), tau=.20)$E[1], numeric(1))
This evaluates the two complete reports at the mixture’s endpoints. Their error counts appear in the vertex table; randomising those reports forms the average point.



Standalone: embed/frontier-mixtures.html, for example ?preset=tb16.
Related applications: The error–disclosure frontier · Reporting risk and withholding cost · Alternative rankings from a posterior distribution.

title: The number of ordered grade reports
text: A grade report partitions units into groups and orders those groups. The set of possible reports therefore includes all strict rankings as well as reports with shared grades. Restrictions on the number of occupied grades, or on the order in which groups may occur, reduce this set. The curves compare the resulting family sizes on a logarithmic scale. The small examples identify the groupings and orders counted as distinct reports. These are combinatorial counts; calculating them does not require evaluating the reporting risk of each candidate.

title: The number of ordered grade reports
text:
Numerical illustrations

Three units. There are 13 ordered grade reports but only 6 strict rankings. In the small examples, some reports group letters, while others give each letter its own box. Swapping the positions of occupied boxes changes which directions are stated.
Six units. All reports number 4,683. A cap permits 603, while an exact grade count permits 540; cuts of one declared order permit only 32. The capped family includes reports with fewer occupied grades, which explains its larger count than the exact family.
Eight units. All reports reach 545,835, compared with 6,051 under the cap and 128 along one order. The dashed lines identify the families even where their counts are close. Arrow-key selection and the table give the exact count for each unit count and family.
Twelve units. There are 28,091,567,595 reports in the full family, while the cap leaves 523,251. The hollow squares mark problem sizes encountered elsewhere in this collection. Counting those possibilities does not require generating every report.
An empty exact family. The small example has 0 reports: the requested number of nonempty grades exceeds its number of units. An empty family has no logarithmic height, so its count stays visible in the table.







A declared order permits only contiguous cuts of that order, without equal-score blocks here. This is a substantive restriction on the available reports. Counts describe family size; they say neither which report has smallest risk nor how long a particular optimisation algorithm will take.



Standalone: report counts, for example ?n=8&G=3.
Related applications: Grade reports as pairwise decisions, Reporting risk and withholding cost.

title: Sensitivity to corrections and unit removal
text: A correction to one unit’s posterior, or removal of a unit from the comparison population, can change reported relations among other units. Grades are selected jointly, so unchanged marginal distributions do not imply unchanged reported comparisons. The two cards use common axes, and the matrix and list identify changed relations between units whose inputs remain fixed. The examples distinguish corrections to a mean or standard deviation from changes in the population. For unit removal, only relations among retained units are compared; numerical grade labels alone do not define the change.

title: Sensitivity to corrections and unit removal
text:
Numerical illustrations

Correct a mean. The list reports 2 of 10 pairs between untouched units changed. The correction moves one site down while rearranging boundaries among other sites. The relation table distinguishes new disclosures from new withholding decisions.
No correction. The original posterior is retained and 0 of 10 untouched pairs change. The two cards describe the same report. Varying the corrected mean identifies the next boundary change.
More uncertainty. Under a tighter grade cap, raising one site’s posterior SD changes 6 of 10 untouched pairs. Their distributions remain exactly as before.
Drop a unit. Removing a site changes 1 of 10 remaining pairs. The relation comparison excludes the removed site and compares directions, rather than numerical grade labels.
Drop U15 from the league. The original card has grade sizes 1, 12, 15, 2; the new card has sizes 9, 17, 3. Among the remaining units, 107 of 406 relations change: 62 newly withheld and 45 newly stated. The expected-rank order is recomputed after removal, and each report is optimal within its own order, with no grade cap.
Two scores, drop C. Equal-weight scores A and B use all reports. Removing C changes 2 of 10 remaining pairs: A–B and A–D become stated. Both marginal-card views show the same common grades; neither score alone chose them.

The unit and reporting settings define further sensitivity comparisons. Correcting a marginal is available for either single score; the two-score and league modes remove a unit. Each before/after pair keeps the same cost and grade policy.






These independent normal posteriors are stipulated for teaching. A correction changes only the selected score’s marginal; a real model refit might change other marginals too. Dropping a unit retains the remaining marginal distributions but changes the population, pair count and possibly the declared order. The display compares relations on common IDs and checks unchanged pair probabilities for every criterion. An excluded unit is unassessed here, not assigned the lowest grade.

get_grades(original)

title: Reporting risk and withholding cost
text: A grade report states directions between grades and withholds comparisons within grades. A wrong direction costs one, and withholding a pair costs τ. Let E denote the expected number of wrong directions, M the number of unordered pairs and N the number of stated pairs. The posterior risk per pair is R_τ = E/M + τ(M − N)/M. The first term is the expected error cost; the second is the withholding cost. The display compares the minimum-risk report in the specified family with a user-supplied report under the same τ.

title: Reporting risk and withholding cost
text:
Numerical illustrations

τ .20, at most 3 grades. The best of 603 reports states 12 of 15 pairs, with risk .0417. The matrix says “2 (A and B; E and F)” for below-τ pairs still withheld. The additional risk of a complete report stating these directions exceeds their isolated-pair saving.
τ .20, no cap. The best of 4,683 reports states 14 of 15 pairs, with risk .0372. Only C–D stays withheld. The change-point strip identifies subsequent changes in disclosure.
τ .40, no cap. The strict order states 15 of 15 pairs; risk .0480 consists entirely of expected wrong directions. The all-withheld bar always ends at τ, because it pays that cost on every pair.
τ .30, no cap. The best report stays the same while its risk becomes .0438. A larger τ changes the charge for every withheld pair. Risk comparisons use the same current τ.

Preset report buttons and grade labels entered in site order specify fixed-report comparisons. Its bar evaluates that fixed report at the current τ. An entered report outside the selected family is identified explicitly; it may beat the capped optimum without belonging to its comparison family.






Six fictional sites from the postrank tutorial, score A only; their normal posteriors are given for teaching. On this slider the uncapped optimum states exactly the pairs whose error is below τ. Risk is an expected cost, not the chance that some direction is wrong. The risk formula follows the postrank theory book, chapters 10–11.









TipIn postrank





library(postrank)
g <- c(A=1L,B=1L,C=2L,D=2L,E=3L,F=3L)
postrank_evaluate(g, pr_tutorial$one, weights=c(score_A=1), tau=.2)$primary_risk
This scores the displayed capped report directly. The package’s solver-based tutorial also reports a floating-point correction to the lower bound; direct fixed-report evaluation needs no solver.



Standalone: open the app, for example ?tau=.2&cap=3&stage=2.
Related applications: The decision for an isolated pair · Grade reports as pairwise decisions.

title: Posterior summaries in a grade report
text: Each report-card row gives a unit’s posterior mean and marginal interval, with colour indicating its grade. Different grades state directions; a shared grade withholds their comparison. The between-grade table averages the error probabilities of the corresponding stated pairs. These averages describe individual pairwise statements, rather than the probability of a joint ordering of entire grades. Sorting within grades changes the presentation without changing the reported relations or risk. The progressive display separates the marginal summaries from the comparisons introduced by each additional grade.

title: Posterior summaries in a grade report
text:
Numerical illustrations

Six sites. The card states 12 of 15 pairs, a share .800, with risk .0417 and expected share wrong .00206. Adjacent-grade comparisons have average errors .0024 and .0038. The purple cells compare these errors with those between distant grades; diagonal entries give grade means.
Reveal by grade. Only Grade 1 is drawn initially; the table says “With one grade shown there is nothing to compare yet.” Displaying another grade introduces the corresponding between-grade comparisons. Later grades retain their coloured bands and numbers while their rows are hidden.
Thirty sites. The card states 303 of 435 pairs, with risk .1603 and expected share wrong .121. Adjacent-grade shares are .2019, .1672 and .0640. A cell averages the errors of its stated pairs; it is not a probability about the grades as wholes.

Within-grade sorting affects only the presentation. Expected rank is a unit’s average position under the posterior, with the top position first. Posterior-mean sorting can rearrange rows within a grade; the report still states no direction between those units. The sort is for reading only and does not change the grades or risk.






These synthetic posteriors are taken as given. Grade 1 declares priority; in the poverty example it means the highest synthetic need. The intervals describe individual units, and their overlap does not determine grades. In these cards the least certain stated comparisons are between adjacent grades. The larger example keeps one expected-rank order and chooses where to cut it into grades; its optimum is restricted to that declared order.

one <- postrank(pr_tutorial$one, tau=.2, G_max=3L, backend="highs", fragility=FALSE)
one$fit$evaluation[c("G", "N", "M", "disclosure_rate")]



The larger dataset is the poverty criterion of pr_example_gaussian, an analytic posterior law. The card layout follows the package’s report-card plot; the between-grade display follows Kline, Rose and Walters, Figure 10 and Section VI.B.

title: Optimal reports along the withholding-cost path
text: For a fixed report, posterior risk is an affine function of the withholding cost. The lower envelope of these functions gives the minimum risk over the selected family at each τ. Intersections on this envelope mark changes in the set of optimal reports. A grade cap can exclude reports that define the unrestricted envelope and hence alter both the path and its minimum risk. The low-cost view resolves the initial changes, including the interval on which withholding every pair is optimal.

title: Optimal reports along the withholding-cost path
text:
Numerical illustrations

Overview. The unrestricted best report states 14 pairs, with risk .0372. The capped comparison gives .0417. The faint lines are fixed reports; the heavy envelope follows their pointwise minimum. Arrow keys identify the reports on the envelope; the table gives their complete intervals.
Before the first bend. The report states 0 of 15 pairs, and risk equals the withholding cost .0005. The low-cost strip includes the all-withheld report that an overview starting farther right would miss. The left boundary is a limit, since the cost is positive.
Small cost, coherent report. The best report states 12 of 15 pairs, including 2 directions whose error exceeds the withholding cost. The list gives the error probability for each newly stated direction. These choices are made jointly, so the path cannot be read as a collection of isolated-pair thresholds.
Exactly at a bend. 2 reports share the smallest risk. Both neighbouring segments include the shared endpoint; the read-out shows the first report under the stated equal-risk tolerance. Moving just beyond the bend changes which line is lowest.
Three-grade cap. At the larger cost the capped report still states 12 of 15 pairs, with risk .0817; the unrestricted comparison gives .0480. Restricting the available grades changes the decision problem even though the posterior and the price of withholding are the same.







These are fictional sites with normal posteriors specified for teaching. The lower panel separately shows equal-mean targets: an endpoint-only optimal report must remain in the path even though its interval has no width.









TipIn postrank





library(postrank)
g <- c(A=1L,B=2L,C=3L,D=3L,E=4L,F=5L)
postrank_evaluate(g, pr_tutorial$one, weights=c(score_A=1), tau=.2)$weighted_risk # .03717176
The call evaluates the displayed report at a fixed cost.



Standalone: the τ path, for example ?tau=.005&zoom=low.
Related applications: Reporting risk and withholding cost, Grade reports as pairwise decisions.

title: Error rates under two denominators
text: Two error rates use the same expected wrong count E but different denominators. KRW’s discordance rate, DR, divides by all M unordered pairs, whereas E/N divides by the N pairs whose directions the report states. For positive N, DR = (N/M) × E/N. The factor N/M is the disclosure share. The paired displays evaluate this identity for a synthetic example and KRW’s archived race card. They show how a low rate over all pairs can coexist with a substantially higher error share among the directions disclosed.

title: Error rates under two denominators
text:
Numerical illustrations

τ .25. The synthetic best report states 14 of 15 pairs, a share .933. DR is .0238, while the expected share wrong among stated pairs is .0255. The two rates are close because almost all pairs are stated.
KRW setting. The race card states 1,324 of 4,656 pairs, a share .284. DR .0387 divides the expected wrong count by all pairs; E/N .136 divides it by the stated pairs. Its KRW risk is −.0227 and its postrank risk is .1818, evaluated on the released probabilities.
All pairs stated. The synthetic report states all 15 pairs. Both rates are .0480 because their denominators coincide. The race card remains fixed as the controls change; its title records the costs at which it was chosen.

The rounded identity uses an approximation sign because multiplying rounded rates need not reproduce the rounded product exactly. A small rate over all pairs can accompany a much larger rate among the pairs a report actually states. Neither rate describes the chance that any error occurs somewhere in the report.






KRW’s archived card statistics and the evaluation on released pair probabilities agree at the displayed digits. The released probabilities differ slightly from KRW’s archived probabilities. The card is evaluated here as a fixed report; no claim is made that it minimises postrank’s risk. Its risk below the cost of withholding every pair implies that its expected error share is below that cost at this setting.

library(postrank)
ev <- postrank_evaluate(c(A=1,B=2,C=3,D=3,E=4,F=5),pr_tutorial$one,weights=c(score_A=1),tau=.25)
ev[c("N","M","E_over_M","E_over_N")]

title: Deciles and quartiles of posterior means
text: Quartiles and deciles partition a posterior-mean order into nearly equal groups, with exact score ties retained. The resulting reports are evaluated on KRW’s discordance-rate and informativeness axes. The archived-card curve uses the same released pair probabilities as the fixed-tier points. In each illustrated comparison, an archived card has both a lower expected wrong-direction rate DR and higher informativeness I. The comparison separates a fixed quantile-grouping convention from selection of grade boundaries under a reporting objective. It evaluates existing cards and does not perform a new optimisation under the released law.

title: Deciles and quartiles of posterior means
text:
Numerical illustrations

Race quartiles, card λ .60. The quartile point has DR .1696 and I .4185. The ringed card has lower DR, .1678, and higher I, .4336. The size patterns distinguish optimised boundary positions from nearly equal tier sizes.
Race deciles, card λ .82. Deciles move to DR .2271 and I .4550, while the selected card reaches .2243 and .4589. More tiers disclose more pairs; that alone does not make them a better tradeoff on both axes.
Gender quartiles, card λ .64. Under the signed male-name contact-gap target, quartiles have DR .1978 and I .3621; the card gives .1908 and .3875. These coordinates concern a different target from the race comparisons.
Gender deciles, card λ .80. Deciles give DR .2525 and I .4042; the card gives .2373 and .4078. The comparison depends on the selected λ. The selected card need not improve both coordinates at every grid setting.







KRW discuss deciles and quartiles in §IV.B and Figure 2C, and reporting possibilities in §V.E and Figure 6. The diamonds are constructed fixed-tier comparisons. The curve joins archived grid cards selected under KRW’s archived probabilities; recomputing their coordinates under the released law supplies no new optimality certificate. KRW write τ̄ for the informativeness axis. Gender remains signed, rather than an absolute contact gap.

Provided as is, without warranty. The data describe KRW’s correspondence experiment, not any firm’s current conduct.

title: Fixed quantile tiers
text: A quantile-tier rule sorts estimates into groups of nearly equal size. Interpreted as an ordered grade report, it states every direction between tiers and withholds every comparison within a tier. The grouping uses the estimates alone; a separately specified posterior evaluates the expected errors of its statements. The display records grade sizes, disclosure and reporting risk, together with individual errors above the withholding cost. A shared tier withholds a comparison. Neither membership in a tier nor its size determines the posterior probability that a particular stated direction is correct.

title: Fixed quantile tiers
text:
Numerical illustrations

Three tiers. Three groups of 10 state 300 of 435 pairs, a share of .690. Under the teaching posterior they expect 51.86 wrong directions, .173 per stated direction, and risk .1813 at τ .20. The marks identify all stated pairs with error above τ, including comparisons across several boundaries.
Ten tiers, marks on. Disclosure rises to 405 pairs (.931), but expected wrong directions rise to 89.40 and E/N to .221. There are 197 marked pairs; the largest stated error is .802. Risk .2193 exceeds the all-withheld report’s .2000 at this τ. This comparison does not make τ an error bound for the tier rule.
Four tiers. Quantile positions produce sizes 8, 7, 8, 7 and state 337 pairs (.775). The grouped formula counts within-tier withheld pairs. The equal-size closed form disappears because four does not divide thirty.
Two tiers. Groups of 15 state 225 pairs (.517). Each within-tier triangle holds comparisons the report leaves unsaid; arrows read every cell of the pair map.
Thirty tiers. Every pair is stated. The tiers follow the estimates, so their 102.2 expected wrong directions differ from the 94.48 of the posterior-mean ranking in Ranking states many claims. With G set to one, E/N becomes “NA: no disclosure,” while risk is .2000.







These are thirty simulated units in one frozen draw, with independent normal teaching posteriors (prior mean 0, SD .15). Tier membership is fixed by the grouping rule. τ changes their evaluation and the marked errors, while their membership stays fixed. The loss evaluates stated directions rather than the purpose a tier rule was designed for. Sizes alone do not determine how many directions are wrong. Quantile sizes are nearly balanced when estimates have no ties; the package merges tiers crossed by equal scores.

Each rule states some directions and withholds others, permitting evaluation under a common posterior and loss. title: Reporting, allocation and classification
text: Selecting the largest posterior expected value differs from selecting the most probable first-ranked unit. A grade report instead determines which pairwise directions to state. The examples evaluate these objectives under one law. Allocation from shared grades requires a further selection rule. Threshold classification depends on exceedance probabilities and false-positive and false-negative costs. Grades alone specify neither decision.

title: Reporting, allocation and classification
text:
Numerical illustrations

Three units, reporting objective. The report has risk .1833. Filling a place from its highest grade selects expected value 4.000 and has top-set overlap .700. The marked native-objective point and risk projections use distinct coordinates.
Three units, mean-value order. Selecting A instead gives value 6.000 but top-set overlap .300; the strict report’s risk is .4667. The top-set order in the table prefers B. Choosing a first recipient does not require publishing every comparison in a strict order.
Two units, τ .25. The reporting optimum withholds. The added allocation lottery still fills a place, giving expected value 5.000 and overlap .500. It draws a whole subset of the required size from the boundary grade, rather than independently including each unit.
False-negative cost 3. The native threshold classifier declares 2 positive, with cost .700. The convention “positive through the highest grade” declares only B positive and costs .900. Neither τ nor the place budget sets the probability cutoff for this decision. Under Threshold 4, being exactly at the substantive threshold does not count as above it. The native classifier declares 0 positive, at cost .300. The grade cutoff permits both none-positive and all-positive decisions: those actions remain distinct even if a canonical grade representation would lose the distinction.
Equal reporting risk, different classifications. Reports 2/1/2 and 3/1/2, in A/B/C order, both have risk .2000. With the same added grade cutoff, they declare 3 and 2 positive, at costs 1.700 and 1.300. Equal reporting risk does not make the added actions equivalent.
League, five places. Mean-score selection gives value .558 and estimated overlap 2.733. The top-set order gives estimated overlap 2.825. These membership probabilities use the displayed posterior draws; their ordering and overlap evaluation use the same draws.







These are synthetic conditional laws. Value is the selected target value, rather than an intervention effect. A grade-based allocation or classification requires a boundary lottery or an eligibility convention. Finite-law quantities are exact; the league’s normal means and threshold probabilities are analytic, while membership and overlap are Monte Carlo estimates. The league reporting optimum covers only capped contiguous cuts of its declared posterior-mean order; the strict comparison reports lie outside that family.



Standalone: one-place, for example ?mode=threshold&falseNegativeCost=3.
Related applications: Restrictions imposed by a fixed order, The decision for an isolated pair.

title: Tiers and optimised cuts of posterior rankings
text: An ordering and a set of grade boundaries impose separate restrictions on a report. Fixed posterior-mean tiers choose both by convention. Optimising the boundaries searches all permitted cuts of the specified posterior-mean or expected-rank order. For eight units, enumeration also provides the minimum over all feasible reports. Each card identifies its search family and disclosure, allowing risk comparisons under a common posterior and withholding cost. The larger examples retain the restriction to one order, so their results do not establish an unrestricted optimum.

title: Tiers and optimised cuts of posterior rankings
text:
Numerical illustrations

Eight units: optimal cuts. Both orders’ cuts state 17 pairs at risk .1455, matching the best of 6,051 reports with at most three grades. Fixed tiers state 21 pairs at risk .1612. This equality between cuts and the joint optimum is a property of these units.
League: fixed tiers. The tiers state 300 pairs at risk .1731. Optimizing their boundaries states 251 at risk .1581. Every rule uses the same posterior and price, but these reports disclose different amounts.
Thirty sites: rank cuts. The cuts state 303 pairs at risk .1603, after searching 4,090 contiguous reports. The orders table shows that the two orders need not coincide for their chosen cuts to agree.
Eight units: all reports. The benchmark expands to 545,835 reports. The reported family determines the scope of the gap for each rule and grade cap.







The tiers are constructed comparators, not optimised reports. When the same order’s tiers belong to its cut family, optimising the boundaries cannot raise risk. Joint optimisation can improve further only within the declared family. The guarantee table separates composite and directional objectives; an optimiser for one need not be best for the other. Larger examples have no joint optimum displayed, so their distance from it is unknown.









TipIn postrank





w <- c(poverty = 1, frl = 0, snap = 0); s <- postrank_settings(weights = w, tau = .25, G_max = 4L)
pm <- postrank_cuts(pr_example_gaussian$means[, "poverty"], pr_example_gaussian, s, direction = "descending", method = "posterior_mean")
c(risk = pm$risk)



Standalone: posterior-tiers, for example ?preset=league8-cuts.
Related applications: Restrictions imposed by a fixed order, Restrictions on the report family.

title: Common withholding cost and matched disclosure
text: Two comparisons use different constraints. At a common withholding cost, posterior risk combines expected errors with the cost of the pairs left unstated. At matched disclosure, the frontier comparison holds the number of stated pairs fixed and compares expected wrong counts. The display evaluates the same rules under both criteria, using one posterior and a specified report family. This makes the source of each risk or error difference explicit. For the thirty-unit example, the boundary is restricted to contiguous cuts of one order.

title: Common withholding cost and matched disclosure
text:
Numerical illustrations

Same τ, .20. Posterior-mean tiers state 21 pairs with risk .1612, while the best report states 17 with risk .1455. These reports disclose different amounts. The solid and dashed lines have the same slope; a lower line has lower risk at this τ.
Same N, eight units. The tiers’ gap is .1634 at N 21. The diamond is a frontier mixture, while the square marks the best single report at that N. The table now compares wrong counts at each rule’s own disclosure.
Thirty units, one order. The capped family has 436 reports. Posterior-mean tiers state 300 pairs with E 48.31. The boundary is optimal within this order; other orders are not searched.
Thirty units, same τ. Without the cap, the family contains 536,870,912 contiguous cuts of the posterior-mean order. There is no enumerated cloud here. Both comparison modes use the same units.
Flags outside the order. The flag report is outside this family: it still has an evaluated risk, but no matched-disclosure benchmark in this order family. The hollow mark records this restriction.
All-withheld. N is 0 and the risk at τ .20 is .2000. Its fraction of stated pairs that are wrong is undefined.







All rules share a supplied normal teaching posterior. Flags use the mean of all thirty estimates as their reference. On thirty units the boundary is the hull of contiguous cuts in one declared order, not the unrestricted H(m). Changing τ changes the loss; changing the family changes the benchmark. Risks across those settings answer different questions. No reporting-risk comparison establishes a rule’s value for allocation or classification.









NoteIn postrank





The package’s synthetic pr_example_gaussian poverty example uses its own thirty sites. At τ .25 with at most four grades, this prints quantile cuts with N 337 and risk .1758, versus optimal cuts with N 303 and risk .1603. The risks correspond to different N; H(m) is not a package output.
w <- c(poverty=1, frl=0, snap=0); s <- postrank_settings(weights=w, tau=.25, G_max=4L); sc <- pr_example_gaussian$means[, "poverty"]
sapply(c("quantile", "optimal"), function(r) unlist(postrank_cuts(sc, pr_example_gaussian, s, direction="descending", rule=r)$evaluation[c("N", "primary_risk")]))

title: Disclosure determined by tier sizes
text: The sizes of the tiers determine the number of stated pairs. All pairs between different tiers are stated, while all within-tier pairs are withheld. The resulting disclosure count depends on the size vector but not on the identities or posterior distributions of the units. The examples compare balanced and unbalanced vectors at fixed unit and tier counts. The distribution enumerates ordered positive size patterns, rather than assignments of labelled units to grades. It therefore describes a combinatorial property of reporting, independently of the accuracy of the directions a particular assignment would state.

title: Disclosure determined by tier sizes
text:
Numerical illustrations

Balanced thirty. Sizes 10, 10, 10 state 300 of 435 pairs, a share of .690. Each withheld triangle contributes its within-tier count to the grouped formula. Balanced sizes reach the maximum for this number of tiers.
Two tiny tiers. Sizes 1, 1, 28 state only 57 pairs, although they use the same number of tiers. The balanced reference still states 300. Moving the smallest tiers to another position gives the same disclosure but another ordered size pattern.
Four tiers. Sizes 8, 7, 8, 7 state 337 pairs (.775). Equal sizes are impossible here. The balanced maximum still exists, while the closed form for equal-sized tiers is hidden.
Balanced twelve. Three groups of four state 48 of 66 pairs. Valid size changes preserve the total unit count; the vector and individual controls specify the same setting.
Unbalanced twelve. Sizes 5, 4, 3 state 47 pairs, below the balanced maximum of 48. A zero size or incorrect total is invalid; the result remains unavailable until the vector is feasible.







The distribution gives equal weight to every ordered positive size vector for the declared unit and tier counts. Its frequencies count size patterns rather than labelled grade reports. All feasible patterns are included; unit assignments are not enumerated. Quantile positions produce nearly balanced sizes when estimates have no ties. The package keeps equal scores together, which can merge tiers and change the realised sizes. The formula’s count of disclosed pairs is exact for any valid sizes, with no posterior or accuracy guarantee.



Standalone: embed/tier-sizes.html, for example ?preset=tiny&theme=dark.
Related applications: Fixed quantile tiers, with the full league, pair map and expected wrong directions; The number of ordered grade reports, which counts assignments to ordered grades.

title: Case-report specification and export
text: Reports are calculated from released probabilities under declared targets, losses and families. Error-budget rows evaluate the displayed report without selecting a constrained alternative. The reporting view retains assumptions, computation scope and conditioning, with drafting and download controls. Browser results are distinguished from archived statuses and bounds.

title: Case-report specification and export
text:
Numerical illustrations

CDE: three-grade family. The browser enumerates all 523,251 capped reports. The chosen report states 45 pairs. The family label, criterion profile and fixed-archive comparison define the reported computation scope. These twelve schools are a deliberately spread teaching subset, not a representative statewide sample.
KRW: equal weights. The report states 636 pairs and is optimal within this order: the weighted expected-rank order. The order and its report family are recomputed when the error weight changes. The supplied marginal intervals describe individual targets; no joint race–gender posterior or Gaussian replacement is created.
Alabama: equal weights. The report states 1,249 pairs. Grade 1 means favourable historical outcomes, including lower incarceration, rather than greatest need. Source conditioning and the supplied interval level stay attached to the case and its model TXT.
CDE: cap two. The family contains 4,095 reports. Its risk and the archived risk use the same withholding cost. Changing a cap changes the family; it does not make same-loss evaluations incomparable.
CDE: mean-order cap four. The computation switches to the posterior-mean order. It is optimal only among cuts of that order. The budget rows still evaluate the displayed report and show signed count-form slack.
CDE: all withheld. E/N reads NA: no disclosure. A homogeneous budget passes without stating anything, so passing alone is not evidence of informative or error-free reporting. The reporting view retains these qualifications in the download.







Current and archived settings appear together; the old status, bound and gap never certify a new browser DP. Shared grades withhold directions, not assert equality; expected error shares do not give joint correctness. Allocation needs another decision rule. Draft text remains in component memory, outside the URL, iframe state and storage.
CDE’s prior conditions on the statewide fit. KRW uses historical contact-gap targets from Kline, Rose and Walters and their data deposit, under the deposit’s CC-BY-NC terms (no version stated); this extraction does not describe current conduct. Alabama uses Opportunity Atlas historical outcomes under CC BY 4.0. Each case retains its complete attribution, changes and conditioning below the app and in downloads.

The mean-order cap-four result states 54 pairs, with risk .0368858. With postrank 1.1.0 loaded:

title: Marginal summaries and joint direction probabilities
text: Under a jointly normal posterior, the larger posterior mean identifies the more probable direction, with or without independence. This property need not hold for other posterior distributions. Moreover, marginal distributions alone do not determine π_AB = Pr(θ_A > θ_B ∣ Y) when dependence is unspecified. The finite examples assign each true value to 0, 1 or 2 and preserve both marginal distributions, but give π_AB = 1/3 under law 1 and 2/3 under law 2. A separate mixture example shows how a component with small probability at a large value can increase A’s mean without producing a correspondingly large direction probability.

title: Marginal summaries and joint direction probabilities
text:
Numerical illustrations

Law 1. Each unit’s own posterior, its row or column total, puts 1/3 on each value, and both posterior means are 1.00, yet π_AB = 1/3 and π_BA = 2/3: B is more probably the higher unit. In the figure, w = .20 puts A’s mean at .120, above B’s 0, yet π_AB = .392.
Law 2. The same totals, paired differently: now π_AB = 2/3. The editable cell counts specify the joint law.
Independent. Every pair once: the totals stay at 1/3, but A equals B with probability 1/3, so π_AB = π_BA = 1/3, adding up to 2/3, not one.
Always equal. The same totals, and A always equals B: π_AB = π_BA = 0. Adding a count to a blue cell changes both the margins and π_AB.
w .50. Two equally weighted mixture components: A’s mean, .450, and π_AB = .620 point the same way. Among the slider’s settings, the two disagree only for w from .10 to .30.







The two laws are restated from the postrank theory book, ch. 9 (Fig. f09b); the posteriors are set by hand, and every probability is computed in this browser. Tie-freeness, that the two true values are never exactly equal, is an assumption about the joint law: with θ_A = θ_B = Z for one continuous Z, both posteriors are continuous, yet A always equals B. postrank’s postrank_mixture_coefficients() averages the pair probabilities over the bumps of such a posterior and does not replace it by one normal posterior.

title: Monte Carlo error with dependent draws
text: Estimation of π_AB from posterior draws must account for dependence. Positive serial correlation in Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) output increases variance relative to independent sampling. The stationary two-state example has equally probable states, A above B and A below B, so π_AB = 1/2. The probability of retaining the current state controls dependence. Exact finite-sample variances and failure probabilities provide references for the simulated chains and independence-based uncertainty measures.

title: Monte Carlo error with dependent draws
text:
Numerical illustrations

Stay .99. Treated as 100 independent draws, the estimate has SD .0500 (its exact SD is .376), and the iid error bound (radius .148) would fail in at most .05 of runs; in these 2,000 chains it fails in .801 (1,602 chains; exact chance .804). A chain that never switches (chance .370) fails by itself.
Stay .99, chain-aware. The SD from the stay chance: .376 (variance .1412) against .0500 (.002500) for independent draws, the variance of 1.77 independent draws (1.01 by the long-run formula, which holds only for long chains). The bands now span almost all of 0 to 1.
A stuck chain. Chain 7 never switches: its estimate is 0 and its iid MCSE is 0, yet π_AB = 1/2. Of these 2,000 chains, 720 never switch.
Stay .50. Independent draws: correlation 0, the variance of 100 independent draws, and the iid error bound fails in 10 of the 2,000 runs (.005; exact .004), well under .05.
1,000 draws. Ten times as many draws give the variance of 10.6 independent draws, and the iid error bound, now of radius .047, still fails in .777 of these chains (exact .770).
postrank’s chains. In pr_toy_mcmc the pooled share is .172 against the known .2, its MCMC MCSE .0576 against .00835 by the iid formula; R-hat 1.0905 and bulk ESS 42.95 flag the slow mixing. The fixed report’s loss is .248 against 4/15 (.191 to .296 by chain).







The two-state chain is restated from the postrank theory book, ch. 15 (“Finite-sample coefficient error in a stationary two-state chain”); the exact numbers come from the stay chance, the counts from chains simulated in this browser. In postrank, postrank_iid_bounds() refuses MCMC draws, and postrank_diagnose() reports R-hat, ESS and an MCMC MCSE for them (vignette m6, “Monte Carlo uncertainty and diagnostics”).

mc <- postrank_draws(pr_toy_mcmc, regime = "mcmc", chains = 4L, warmup_per_chain = 0L, thin = 1L, declarations = law$declarations)
postrank_diagnose(mc, pairs = data.frame(entity_i = "A", entity_j = "B", criterion_id = "k1"))$summaries$pair_1$diagnostics   # values: rhat 1.090465, ess_bulk 42.95484, mcse_mean 0.05764243 (1.0905, 42.95, .0576)

title: Majority comparisons and expected ranks
text: The majority-win count Hᵢ = #{j:Pr(θᵢ > θⱼ ∣ Y) > 1/2} counts the opponents that unit i is more likely to exceed. Expected rank instead sums the probabilities of being exceeded: R̄ᵢ↓ = 1 + ∑_j≠i Pr(θⱼ > θᵢ ∣ Y). For independent normal posteriors, the majority-win count gives the posterior-mean ordering. Other posterior laws need not have this property. The examples compare these summaries with KRW’s cards at λ = 1, where correct and incorrect directions have equal reward and cost.

title: Majority comparisons and expected ranks
text:
Numerical illustrations

Law on orders. A beats B and C, each only with probability .51; B’s one win is nearly sure (.99). Majority wins put A first, the expected rank B (1.52 against A’s 1.98).
League. Majority wins give the posterior-mean order: 0 of the 435 pairs differ. The expected-rank order states 6 pairs against the majority; U13 is 8th by it (9.59) and 6th by the other two.
League, prior SD .30. Still 0 of the 435 pairs; the expected-rank order now states 12 pairs against the majority.
KRW, race. Majority wins form a strict order. Against it the posterior-mean order states 35 of the 4,656 pairs and the expected-rank order 62; KRW’s card at λ = 1 states none against it, so no full ranking expects fewer wrong claims: 1,248, against 1,249 for the posterior-mean order.
KRW, gender. Macy’s beats Jones Lang LaSalle (.5008), which beats Dollar General (.5022), which beats Macy’s (.5014): a cycle, and the three win 45 pairs each. KRW’s card at λ = 1 (96 grades) puts Macy’s and Dollar General in one grade, within KRW’s solver tolerances.







KRW call the grades at λ = 1 Condorcet ranks (Section II.F). Their remark there that the count of wins is equivalent to the posterior mean rank (the expected rank) does not hold in general: on the race gaps, majority wins and the expected rank order 62 pairs differently. The data describe KRW’s correspondence experiment, not any firm’s current conduct. Data: Kline, Rose and Walters (2024), A Discrimination Report Card, American Economic Review, doi:10.1257/aer.20230700; deposit doi:10.3886/E198284V1; CC-BY-NC as stated by the deposit (no version), noncommercial use only. Pair probabilities as adapted in postrank 1.1.0 (pr_case_krw). Cards computed with KRW’s code (KRW replication companion) under KRW’s archived pair probabilities (KRW’s cards along λ). Changes noted; no endorsement by the authors is implied.

w <- rowSums(e < t(e), na.rm = TRUE); pm <- postrank_posterior_means(r)[, 1]; er <- postrank_expected_rank(r)
c(mean = sum(outer(w, w, ">") & outer(pm, pm, "<")), rank = sum(outer(w, w, ">") & outer(er, er, ">")))   # 35 62

title: Estimates and sampling error
text: Consider an estimate equal to a fixed true value plus normally distributed sampling error. Repeated data collection produces different estimates of the same quantity. The standard error (SE) is the standard deviation of this sampling distribution; approximately two-thirds of the estimates fall within one SE of the true value. The simulation displays successive estimates and decomposes the most recent estimate into its true value and sampling error. The Draw control generates a further observation from this distribution.

title: Estimates and sampling error
text:
Numerical illustrations

SE .20. Twenty estimates of a unit whose true value is .50: 12 of 20 fall within one SE (the filled dots), against 13.65 expected on average. The ringed latest estimate, .229, is the true value plus noise −.271.
200 draws. With ten times as many draws, the count within one SE moves from 12 of 20 to 132 of 200, against 136.54 expected, while the share expected on average stays .6827.
Seed 2. The same unit with other data: this time 18 of 20 estimates fall within one SE. The count moves from one set of data to the next; the expected 13.65 does not.
SE .10. Seed 1 again with half the SE: every estimate moves halfway toward the true value and the noise arrow halves to −.136, yet each draw keeps its noise in SEs (−1.36), so the count stays 12 of 20.
SE .05. Halving the SE again gives the same standardised errors: the noise is −.068, and still 12 of 20 fall within one SE. The three SEs are those of the small, medium and large units in Ranking noisy estimates.







The simulation specifies a fixed true value for one unit. Each estimate is the true value plus the SE times a draw from the normal curve, taken from a seeded stream, so a seed always gives the same estimates. This is the model of Kline, Rose and Walters (2024), Section III, Assumption 1 (stated before Section III.A), and talk slide 17. Walters’ Mixtape slides (pp. 5–6) set it up the same way, and the postrank theory book, ch. 2, “Teacher growth categories: evidence, precision, and the choice of assessment”, reads estimates together with their standard errors.

title: Interval overlap across 435 pairs
text: The thirty units of the simulated league yield 435 unordered pairs. Their posterior intervals are calculated under the normal model used in normal–normal posterior shrinkage. For each selected pair, the display gives the interval overlap and the posterior probability that the first unit has the larger true value. The table distinguishes non-overlapping intervals from overlapping intervals with, or without, a direction probability above .90. This classification quantifies the extent to which interval overlap coexists with relatively high posterior support for one direction. It also permits comparisons across interval levels and prior standard deviations.

title: Interval overlap across 435 pairs
text:
Numerical illustrations

Overlap, highest probability. 399 of the 435 pairs have overlapping 90% intervals, and 88 of them still have one direction above .90. The highest is .988, for U13 above U05, whose intervals overlap by .005: no overlapping pair is above .99.
U06 and U20. These intervals do not overlap (.002 lies between them), and U06 is the higher with probability .988, the same to three decimals as the overlapping pair above: the two comparisons have similar posterior support despite different overlap classifications.
U04 and U18. A wide overlap, .107, and still U04 is the higher with probability .904: U18’s narrow interval ends at −.105, below U04’s posterior mean, −.014.
95% intervals. Wider intervals overlap more often, in 413 pairs, and 102 of these have one direction above .90. The highest is now .997, for U03 above U15.
Prior SD .05. A narrow prior pulls every posterior mean toward zero: 427 pairs overlap, only 58 of them with one direction above .90.







For two independent normal posteriors, whatever their SDs, the more likely direction has a probability above .950 when their 90% intervals do not overlap. When they overlap, it is at most .990, the value for equal SDs and intervals that just touch (.975 and .997 for 95% intervals). Kline, Rose and Walters (2024, section IV.C) draw a credible interval beside each name, but they grade the names from pairwise posterior probabilities.

title: From data to posterior decisions
text: Posterior reporting involves four stages: observed data Y, a model and prior, the posterior distribution Pr(θ ∣ Y), and a decision expressed as a grade report. The analyst specifies the model and computes the posterior using other software. postrank takes this posterior as input and selects the report. The diagram identifies the quantities and responsibilities at each stage. A two-unit example provides the corresponding calculations, and the table describes the operations available for the different posterior representations accepted by postrank.

title: From data to posterior decisions
text:
Numerical illustrations

Box 1 (Data). Y holds the estimates and their SEs: .25 (SE .10) for A and .05 (SE .20) for B. postrank never reads Y itself, only a posterior computed from it.
Box 2 (Model). The prior SD, .15, is the analyst’s choice, set by hand here. With each SE it sets how much of its estimate each posterior mean keeps: .692 for A, .360 for the noisier B.
Box 3 (Posterior). The posterior is the input to postrank. The posterior means are .173 and .018, and π = .856 is the probability that A is truly higher. B more precise (SE .10, as for A): B keeps .692 too, its mean is .035, and π rises to .880.
Box 4 (Decision). The postrank step: stating A above B is wrong with probability .144, less than τ = .20, so postrank states it, {A} > {B}, the best of all 3 reports. At τ .10 withholding costs less than .144, so postrank withholds the pair: {A, B}.
Prior SD .05. With a narrower prior, A’s posterior mean falls to .050 and π to .762. Stating A above B would now be wrong with probability .238, so postrank withholds the pair: {A, B}. The change in grades results from the altered model specification and its posterior probabilities.







Kline, Rose and Walters (2024), Section III.A–B, set out the empirical Bayes posteriors behind their firm grades (KRW call them beliefs). In their talk, slides 34 and 37 show the model for first names, not for the firms; slides 43 to 52 set out the empirical Bayes model for the firms. Walters’ Mixtape slides on empirical Bayes (p. 13) set out the same recipe. The two units here are set by hand, and the browser computes their posterior; postrank fits no model.
