title: Sensitivity to the prior standard deviation
text: The prior standard deviation determines the amount of shrinkage in the normal–normal model. It may be specified by the analyst or estimated from the data by an empirical Bayes procedure. Four panels evaluate the simulated league from normal–normal posterior shrinkage over prior standard deviations from .01 to 1 on a logarithmic scale. With the prior centred on the average true value, the posterior means have the smallest average squared error near the standard deviation of those values. Pairwise posterior probabilities also vary with the prior specification; Pairwise posterior direction probabilities defines the probability used in these comparisons.

title: Sensitivity to the prior standard deviation
text:
Numerical illustrations

Near the true spread. At prior SD .15 both distance curves are at their lowest point among the slider’s settings: .0096 in this draw (the estimates: .0163) and .0075 over many draws. A finer search puts the closed form’s lowest point at about .146, next to the true spread, .149.
Much too narrow. At .02 the posterior means end farther from the true values than the estimates: .0197 against .0163 in this draw, .0191 against .0175 over many draws. In this draw the posterior puts one direction above .90 in only 6 of the 435 pairs.
Too narrow. At .05 the expected pairs against the true order are 87.45, against 88.12 for the estimates and 80.66 at their fewest; in this draw 17 units end farther than their estimates were.
Too wide. At .45 the expected distance is .0133, as at .05, yet in this draw the posterior puts one direction above .90 in 159 pairs instead of 66. These are the posterior’s own probabilities; whether such directions are right under the true values is checked in Reported error and reference-law evaluation. In this draw 13 units end farther, as at every prior SD from about .23 on.
Another draw. With seed 20261031 this draw’s distance is lowest at .12 (.0092); over many draws it stays lowest at .15 (.0075).







“Over many draws” means the closed form: the expectation over draws of the estimates with the true values fixed, not over true values drawn from the prior. The postrank theory book (ch. 18) calls this a fixed-parameter experiment. postrank fits no model and reads the posterior it is given (ch. 18, “Hyperparameters, precision and represented uncertainty”). The best report at each prior SD and the error share it claims are shown in Reported error and reference-law evaluation. The normal–normal shrinkage follows Walters’ Mixtape slides (p. 27).

title: Pairwise posterior direction probabilities
text: Suppose that the true values of units A and B have independent normal posterior distributions. Their pairwise ordering is described by π_AB = Pr(θ_A > θ_B ∣ Y). This is the posterior probability that A has the larger true value, obtained by integrating the distribution of A − B above zero. The figure displays this distribution on the same scales as the two marginal distributions. Independence implies that the variance of the difference is the sum of the marginal variances, so uncertainty in both true values contributes to the comparison.

title: Pairwise posterior direction probabilities
text:
Numerical illustrations

Means .30 and .10, SDs .20 and .20. The two posteriors overlap substantially, while π_AB = .760. The gap is measured against the SD of the difference, .283, not against one unit’s SD: A’s mean is .707 SDs of the difference above B’s.
Means .30 and .10, SDs .20 and .60 (B much less precise). The same gap, but the difference widens to SD .632, so A’s mean is only .316 SDs of it above B’s, and π_AB falls to .624, closer to one half.
Means .20 and .20, SDs .20 and .40. With equal means each direction has probability .500, for either choice of marginal SDs; the difference keeps mean 0 and only spreads out (SD .447).
Means 1.20 and .95, SDs .20 and .20 (tutorial sites A and B). Sites A and B of the six fictional sites in postrank’s tutorial data: π_AB = .812. The package stores one minus this number, the chance that stating A above B would be wrong.







The formula holds for two independent normal posteriors, set here by hand. For them, whatever their SDs, the larger posterior mean is always the more likely direction, and π_BA = 1 − π_AB, because the two true values have probability zero of being equal. Kline, Rose and Walters (2024), section II.E, Example 1, and slide 27 of their talk, use the special case of this formula with both SDs equal to 1.

1 - pr_tutorial$one$e["A", "B", "score_A"]   # 0.8116204: tutorial sites A and B, one minus the stored error

title: Selection bias at the extremes of a ranking
text: Selection by an extreme estimate also selects on sampling error. In a simulation of thirty units, the estimates of the highest-ranked units therefore exceed their true values on average. The corresponding bias for the lowest-ranked units has the opposite sign. Repeated datasets quantify these differences for the selected k units. Under a normal prior centred on the average true value, with a standard deviation near their spread, posterior means substantially reduce the average upward bias of the highest estimates; the remaining average difference is −.007 in this example.

title: Selection bias at the extremes of a ranking
text:
Numerical illustrations

Top 3. Over the 2,000 replays, estimate minus true value averages .160 for the top 3 by estimate; for their posterior means at prior SD .15, near the true values’ spread of .149, it averages −.007. Replay 1 is the draw that 1.3 and 1.5 show first: .071 and −.031.
Replay 9. The repeated-sampling result does not hold in every dataset: here the top 3 sit below their true values (−.043, averaged over the three), and their posterior means further below (−.117). This bias is defined by the average over repeated datasets.
Top 1. Over the replays, the largest estimate overshoots most: .220 above its unit’s true value on average, against .081 for the top 10 (set k to 10). Its posterior mean averages −.024.
Bottom 3. The lower-tail comparison has the opposite sign: on average over the replays the bottom 3 sit below their true values, −.150, and their posterior means have average difference −.013.
Prior SD .05. A prior narrower than the true spread induces excessive shrinkage: on average over the replays the top 3’s posterior means end at −.131, below their true values (at prior SD .10, −.063).







Walters (2024, Handbook of Labor Economics, section 3.5) points to the upward bias of the largest estimate that the ranking step creates. Andrews, Kitagawa and McCloskey (2024, “Inference on Winners”) give inference on the top unit’s value that accounts for it. The posterior here comes from one normal prior set by hand for teaching; postrank does not fit it, and postrank’s input is a posterior, not a list of estimates. With real units the true values are unknown, so this check is not possible.
